# Configuration reference

<!-- Generated by tools/gen_docs.py; do not edit by hand. Regenerate with `make docs`. -->

Every setting the program reads, with its packaged default and the comment written beside
it in `initialize_claude_ai/data/`. Override any of them as described in
[Configuration](configuration.md): a config file, `INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_<SECTION>__<KEY>`, or
`--set section.key=value`. Defaults spanning several lines are shortened here (…);
the TOML file is the authority.

### `[paths]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `state_dir` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_STATE_DIR:-${XDG_STATE_HOME:-${HOME}/.local…` | Where initialize-claude-ai keeps its own state (env.json, logs, generated bridges). |
| `claude_home` | `"${CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR:-${HOME}/.claude}"` | Claude Code's own configuration directory. |
| `work_dir` | `"${cfg:paths.state_dir}/work"` | Scratch space for downloads, generated MCP bridges and sandboxed installs. |
| `log_file` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_LOG_FILE:-claude_ai_initialization.log}"` | The run's own record: every line printed on screen and every log record underneath it, in one file, in the order they happened. Empty means "do not record"; --log-file FILE points it elsewhere and --no-log-file turns it off. Relative, so it lands in the directory the command was run from rather than somewhere under ~/.local/state that has to be looked up first: the log is for the person watching the install, and it should be where they already are. Give an absolute path here (or in INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_LOG_FILE) to pin it instead. |
| `extra_bin_dirs` | `[ …` | Extra directories searched for binaries, ahead of PATH. |

### `[environment]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `demote_echo` | `true` |  |
| `echo_files` | `[ …` | The settings files Claude Code merges and re-exports, user scope then project scope. Named here rather than in code so another host layout is a config edit. |
| `echo_key` | `"env"` | The key inside those files that holds the exported block. |
| `echo_names` | `[ …` | Names eligible for it, as shell-style patterns: the coordinates this program writes and would otherwise read back. An allow list rather than "everything in the block", so a variable the operator put there for their own reasons keeps working the way it always did. |
| `echo_keep` | `[ …` | ... except these, whatever the patterns above say. A credential kept in the settings file is the only copy there is: demoting it would not correct a stale answer, it would lose the answer. Phase 2 goes on seeing it exactly as before. |

### `[logging]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `level` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_LOG_LEVEL:-info}"` | Verbosity on screen. The file keeps file_level regardless, so --quiet and a raised level still leave a complete record behind in paths.log_file. |
| `file_level` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_LOG_FILE_LEVEL:-debug}"` |  |
| `format` | `"%(asctime)s %(levelname)-7s %(name)s: %(message)s"` |  |
| `date_format` | `"%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S"` | Shared by the log records and the per-run header in the log file. |
| `record_output` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_LOG_RECORD_OUTPUT:-true}"` | Mirror the console -- banners, status lines, summary boxes, the JSON report -- into paths.log_file alongside the log records. false records only what was logged, which is the behaviour of an ordinary log file. |
| `badges` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_LOG_BADGES:-true}"` | Render each log record's level on screen as the same badge the report uses, so a WARNING on stderr and a [PARTIAL] step on stdout look alike in the one scrollback they share. Affects the terminal only; the file keeps the plain 'format' above, because a record that has to be grepped in six months should not have a sign in front of it. false gives the terminal that plain form too. |
| `max_bytes` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_LOG_MAX_BYTES:-5000000}"` | Roll the log over once it passes this size, keeping this many older copies (claude_ai_initialization.log.1, .2, ...). Checked when the file is opened, so no run rotates out from under itself. 0 for either means "never rotate". |
| `backups` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_LOG_BACKUPS:-3}"` |  |

### `[console]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `glyphs` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_CONSOLE_GLYPHS:-auto}"` | Frame characters: auto \| unicode \| ascii. 'auto' asks the output stream whether it can encode a box-drawing character and falls back to ASCII when it cannot, which is what happens on a host still in the C/POSIX locale. |
| `timestamps` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_CONSOLE_TIMESTAMPS:-true}"` | Put the date and time in front of every line that records something happening -- on screen and in the log file, in logging.date_format, which is the format the log records already use.  Without it the transcript interleaves stamped detail with unstamped narration and the two cannot be lined up, so the file cannot answer "how long did that stage take?" about its own contents. Structural lines are never stamped, whatever this says: the frames and interiors of boxes, table rows, blank lines and the --json report.  A box is one event rather than a line each, its alignment depends on its width, and a stamp repeated down the side of a summary would be twenty copies of the same second.  The heading that introduces a section carries the time instead. |
| `palette` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_CONSOLE_PALETTE:-auto}"` | Colour palette: auto \| vibrant \| daylight \| contrast \| soft \| basic ('classic', 'standard' and 'ansi' are accepted as other names for 'basic', which is the eight-colour scheme most terminal colour guides publish: green pass, red fail, amber caveat, cyan in flight, bold blue heading, dim detail). 'vibrant' is the default. Four of its six hues are at the full chroma of the 256-colour cube -- emerald, amber, cyan -- so the report is properly coloured rather than tinted grey, and every one of them still measures between 7:1 and 11.7:1 against a dark terminal: well clear of the 4.5:1 at which text stops being readable, and short of the neon corners (#00ff00 is 15:1) that make people turn colour off. 'contrast' is the same six meanings with that chroma traded for an even weight -- a tighter 7:1-10:1 band, calmer over an hour where 'vibrant' is quicker to scan in ten seconds. 'daylight' is the design inverted for a light background, where being too pale rather than too bright is what makes a colour unreadable. 'soft' is the quiet one; 'basic' is the plain eight colours, used where 256-colour escapes would print as literal text. 'auto' picks 'vibrant' -- or 'daylight' when COLORFGBG says the background is light -- wherever COLORTERM or a 256-colour TERM says the terminal can render it, and 'basic' where it cannot. In every palette the hue means the same thing, and never carries the meaning alone: each line also states its status in words. Preview them all with `initialize-claude-ai palette`. Colour is turned off entirely by --no-color, NO_COLOR or a non-tty. |
| `width` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_CONSOLE_WIDTH:-80}"` | Total width of rules, banners and summary boxes, in columns. Kept fixed rather than read from the terminal so that piped output and captured logs line up with what was on screen. |
| `decorate` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_CONSOLE_DECORATE:-true}"` | Draw the frames at all. false collapses every banner and summary box to plain unframed lines, for log scrapers and for anyone who prefers it that way. |
| `progress` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_CONSOLE_PROGRESS:-true}"` | Print a cyan [RUNNING] line before the few steps that can take a minute with nothing to show -- a package install, a phase-4 stage, a subagent turn. Only those: a running line for every step would double the length of the report to say what the verdict line says a moment later. false leaves only the verdicts. |
| `max_named_steps` | `12` | Longest step-name list rendered in a summary before it is elided with a count. Keeps a 200-step phase-1 run from burying its own verdict. |

### `[run]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `continue_on_partial` | `true` | Continue to the next phase when one reports 'partial'. --no-partial-success is the command-line form of setting this to false. |
| `continue_on_failure` | `false` | Continue even when a phase fails outright (useful for --json audits). --ignore-failure is the command-line form of setting this to true. |
| `partial_is_failure` | `false` | Make 'partial' a non-zero exit status. |
| `default_phases` | `["all"]` | Phases run when --phases is not given. 'all' is every registered phase, so a phase added later is included without anyone remembering to edit this list. |
| `command_timeout_seconds` | `600` | Per-command default timeout, seconds. Downloads override this individually. |
| `stop_signals` | `["TERM", "KILL"]` | What happens when a command outruns that timeout. The child is started in a session of its own, so these signals go to it and to everything it started, in order, each followed by stop_grace_seconds of waiting. If the last one goes unanswered the child is abandoned rather than waited on: a timeout has to mean the run continues, and a grandchild holding an inherited pipe open must not be able to turn a 900-second limit into an overnight stall. |
| `stop_grace_seconds` | `5` |  |
| `deadline_seconds` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_TIMEOUT:-0}"` | --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # The two global time controls.  Both are off by default and both are no-ops when absent: a run with neither behaves exactly as it did before they existed. --------------------------------------------------------------------------- # A wall-clock ceiling for the whole run, in seconds; 0 means none, which is the default.  --timeout takes suffixes (45s, 90m, 2h, 1d) and writes seconds here. This is not the same thing as a timeout and cannot be built out of them.  Every operation is already bounded -- a probe at 8 seconds, a stage at 180, an agent turn at 900 -- and phase 4 still took 259 minutes against thirteen addresses, because that is what a few hundred well-behaved operations add up to. It stops *admission*, not work in progress: an address that has already begun is left to finish, because killing an agent mid-turn throws away tokens already spent.  So the run can overrun by as long as one address takes.  The verdict is PARTIAL and the report names every address that was never attempted. Named deadline_seconds rather than timeout_seconds on purpose: timeout_scale below matches on that suffix, and the one duration that must never be scaled is the ceiling you typed.  A different name is a better guard than an exception list, because nobody has to remember to maintain it. |
| `timeout_scale` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_TIMEOUT_SCALE:-1.0}"` | Multiplies every per-operation timeout; 1.0 is as written, which is the default.  This is the honest form of "one global timeout value": the timeouts here span 5 seconds (a TCP connect) to 1800 (waiting for a person at a browser), so one value *substituted* everywhere would kill agent turns at 30 seconds or leave dead connections hanging for half an hour.  Multiplying keeps the relationships and answers the question people actually have -- this machine, or this link, is slower than you assumed.  Useful with --concurrency, where several addresses contend for the same CPU and network. |
| `timeout_scale_suffixes` | `["timeout_seconds"]` | Which settings timeout_scale applies to, matched against the *last* segment of the key -- most timeouts are read through a section view and have no full path to match.  The suffix is what keeps the five look-alikes out: progress_interval_ seconds is a heartbeat, latency_target_seconds and latency_ceiling_seconds are thresholds for *scoring* a server when ranking (stretching those would change which server wins), stop_grace_seconds is the SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL gap, and timeout_turn_scale is itself a multiplier.  None of them ends in this suffix. |

### `[machine_env]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | One writer for every per-machine variable (core/machine_env.py): a value that belongs to this machine -- the CA bundle Claude Code needs to trust an internal root, a raised start-up wait, a runtime setting -- is brought to the same end state in every place a new terminal's Claude Code reads.  A line commented out is uncommented, a missing one added (in this program's marked block), a wrong one corrected in place (also when another tool wrote it), a right one recognised.  Every place and its outcome is logged on every run; nothing of it goes into .mcp.json.  openqa-example-net failed with UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY while ~/.bashrc and ~/.profile exported a NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS naming a deleted /tmp file. |
| `places` | `["settings", "~/.bashrc", "~/.profile", "/etc/profile.d/initialize-…` | "settings" is Claude Code's settings.json env; the rest are shell files.  A place the run may not write (/etc/profile.d without root) is reported with the exact line to add. |
| `places_if_present` | `["~/.bash_profile", "~/.bash_login", "~/.zshrc", "~/.zprofile"]` | Written too when they exist: a login bash reads ~/.bash_profile instead of ~/.profile when there is one. |
| `scan` | `["/etc/profile", "/etc/profile.local", "/etc/bash.bashrc", "/etc/ba…` | Startup files scanned for a line that already sets the variable: each one found is a place too, corrected in place.  Another installer had written /etc/profile.d/node_extra_ca_certs.sh exporting a deleted /tmp bundle, which a login shell read after everything else. |
| `block_begin` | `"# >>> initialize-claude-ai: per-machine values (managed; see its l…` |  |
| `block_end` | `"# <<< initialize-claude-ai: per-machine values <<<"` |  |
| `backup` | `true` |  |
| `backup_suffix` | `"%Y%m%d-%H%M%S"` |  |
| `check_effective` | `true` | Afterwards each shell is asked what it ends with: a later line or file can undo an earlier one.  {probe} prints the variable after a marker. |
| `shell_timeout_seconds` | `20.0` |  |
| `say_on_console` | `true` |  |

## 10-components

Source: [`initialize_claude_ai/data/10-components.toml`](../initialize_claude_ai/data/10-components.toml)

### `[install]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `default_groups` | `["base", "runtime", "claude", "cloud", "browser"]` | Component groups selected by default. Override with --install-only / --install-skip / this key. |
| `only` | `[]` | --install-only / --install-skip, made permanent. Component keys or group names; 'only' wins over default_groups, and the command line wins over both. |
| `skip` | `[]` |  |
| `optional_groups` | `["browser", "desktop", "mcp-tooling", "mcp-runtimes"]` | Groups that are nice to have; a failure never fails the phase. |
| `prefetch` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_INSTALL_PREFETCH:-launchers}"` | --install-prefetch: also install, now, the toolchains phase 4 launches MCP servers with, so it does not find them missing later. none       only the groups selected above launchers  plus the component behind the first word of every command in demand_sources below (npx -> npm, uvx -> uv, ...), except a component whose entry says prefetch = false all        plus every component in prefetch_groups, prefetch = false or not What is added this way is always optional: it never fails the phase. --install-only wins over this (it names exactly what to install), and --install-skip wins over everything. |
| `demand_sources` | `["mcp.packages.launchers", "mcp.bridge.adapters"]` | Settings whose values are command templates (argument vectors) that a later phase runs. Read, never changed: adding a launcher there is all it takes for 'launchers' above to prefetch whatever runs it. |
| `prefetch_groups` | `["mcp-runtimes"]` | The groups 'all' above adds. |
| `on_demand_default` | `true` | Whether phase 4 may install a component on demand (--mcp-provision-missing) when its catalog entry does not say. An entry's own on_demand wins. |
| `bin_dir_query_timeout_seconds` | `25` | Seconds allowed for asking a tool where it puts the programs it installs (a component's bin_dir_queries, e.g. `go env GOPATH`). |
| `python_executable` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_INSTALL_PYTHON:-python3}"` | Which interpreter the Python-module checks import with.  Normally the detected one is used and this is never consulted; it is here for a machine where the interpreter that should own the SDKs is not the one on PATH.  Left as the bare name because that is what this has always fallen back to -- naming it here at least makes the fallback visible and overridable rather than a literal buried in install/verify.py. |
| `refresh_package_index` | `true` | Refresh package metadata once before the first system install. |
| `package_timeout_seconds` | `900` | Seconds allowed for a single package-manager transaction. |
| `download_timeout_seconds` | `600` | Seconds allowed for a download or install script. |
| `venv_timeout_seconds` | `300` | Seconds allowed for creating venv_path below. |
| `version_timeout_seconds` | `25` | Seconds allowed for asking a tool its version (a component's version_args). |
| `python_probe_timeout_seconds` | `30` | Seconds allowed for asking an interpreter where packages go, and for the import check that proves a Python component loads. |
| `python_import_timeout_seconds` | `60` |  |
| `python_target` | `"auto"          # auto \| system \| venv \| user` | Where python packages go. auto    system, unless the interpreter is marked externally managed under PEP 668 -- openSUSE, Debian, Fedora, Arch and Homebrew all are -- in which case a virtualenv, which is the one target that installs without arguing with the distro's package manager. system  into the interpreter itself, --user unless already in a virtualenv venv    always venv_path, created from the interpreter running this program user    always pip --user (uv has no equivalent, so pip is used) |
| `venv_path` | `"${cfg:paths.state_dir}/venv"` | Built with the interpreter running initialize-claude-ai, not with whichever python3 is first on PATH: phase 4 imports claude_agent_sdk in-process, and a wheel with a compiled extension will not load across minor versions. |
| `allow_break_system_packages` | `false` | --break-dependencies: install into a PEP-668 externally managed interpreter anyway (Homebrew, openSUSE, Fedora, Debian). Ignored inside a virtualenv, where nothing is being broken. |
| `force` | `false` | --force-install: run the install strategies even when verification already passes, in each manager's reinstalling form. Slow and bandwidth-hungry; the point is to repair a half-installed or corrupted toolchain. |
| `downgrade` | `false` | --downgrade: resolve pip/npm package names through [install.pins] below. |
| `prefer_uv` | `true` | Prefer 'uv pip' when uv is available (much faster, same semantics). |
| `reinstall_owner_only` | `true` | --force-install repairs the copy in use, through whoever installed it: the package that owns the file or provides the command, a strategy whose own folders hold it (owns_paths, adds_bin_dir), or a kind recognised from the path ([install.ownership]).  Strategies that would install a second copy beside it are not run; an owner with no in-place form (reinstall_argv / reinstall_shell) keeps what is there.  npm's "npm22" on a machine with npm26, gcloud's script refusing its own folder, and nvm putting a second node beside /usr/bin/node all came from rerunning fresh-install recipes.  false: every strategy in catalog order, as before. |
| `changed_needs_proof` | `true` | A reinstall is CHANGED only when the binary in use changed (its file, inode, change time or version); otherwise "reported success, but the copy in use did not change" -- node was CHANGED while nothing had touched /usr/bin/node. |
| `check_space` | `true` | What a step costs in disk is asked before it runs.  A reinstall needs the folder holding the copy times its strategy's space_factor (one that stages a copy beside it declares 2), or the installed size of its owning packages (<mgr>.installed_size), plus space_margin_mb; one that does not fit is not run -- "kept", reported OK.  A fresh install with less than space_margin_mb free where it writes is not attempted.  gcloud's in-place reinstall filled a disk with just over 1 GB free, and every later step failed. |
| `space_margin_mb` | `256` |  |
| `clean_failed_step_leftovers` | `true` | What a failed reinstall left next to the folder it owns is removed only when it carries this program's marker (owned_marker): a name proves nothing. gcloud's own reinstall built google-cloud-sdk.staging, failed activating it, and the staging copy was deleted by its name -- gcloud was gone.  Folders another tool left are reported, never deleted. |
| `deleting_needs_ownership` | `true` |  |
| `owned_marker` | `".initialize-claude-ai-owned"` |  |
| `restore_after_failed_step` | `true` | A failed step must leave the tool working: when it worked before and does not now, a runnable copy the step left beside it (its staging, the tool's own backup) is put back; what stood there is kept as <folder>.broken-<time>.  A copy runs when `<tool> tool_runs_args` exits 0. |
| `tool_runs_args` | `["--version"]` |  |
| `tool_runs_timeout_seconds` | `60.0` |  |
| `stop_on_full_disk` | `true` | The first command that hits a full disk stops the phase: the remaining components are "not attempted: the disk is full", and one verdict names it. A full disk is blamed only on the step whose own command hit it. |
| `progress_line_pattern` | `'^[\s#=>.*-]*(\d{1,3}(\.\d+)?%)?[\s#=>.*-]*$'` | Lines left out of an installer's own last words (progress bars, percentages). |
| `script_web_page_markers` | `["<!doctype html", "<html", "<head>", "<body"]` | A downloaded "install script" that starts with one of these is a web page, never run: claude.ai/install.sh once served HTML, and bash ran it. |
| `demand_from_entries` | `true` | What the MCP servers Claude Code starts from here run is installed too: the command of every entry in ./.mcp.json and in Claude Code's own configuration (local and user scope), and what a client bridge runs for every call (its manifest's client).  Only when this machine lacks it, from this catalog -- or a client's own `install` steps ([mcp.discovery.clients.<name>]) -- and optional like any prefetch; a component with prefetch = false is checked, never installed.  What nothing here installs is named with the run that finds or replaces its server.  A copied .mcp.json named github-mcp-server and a client bridge called osc on a machine that had neither. |
| `portable_launchers` | `true` | Before that: an entry launched through an installer's private launcher (a `uv tool` or pipx environment, an npm global module -- mcp.launch_form) is rewritten to the package's portable launch (uvx / npx -y) when that launcher is here.  bugzilla-opensuse-org ran another machine's .../uv/tools/mcp-bugzilla/bin/mcp-bugzilla, a script bound to that install, and could never start where .mcp.json was copied. |

## 20-auth

Source: [`initialize_claude_ai/data/20-auth.toml`](../initialize_claude_ai/data/20-auth.toml)

### `[auth]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `available` | `["google-cloud", "claude-oauth", "anthropic-api"]` |  |
| `backends` | `["all"]` | Which backends to attempt. "all" == every entry in `available`. |
| `required` | `[]` | Backends that must succeed for the phase to pass. Empty means "at least one". |
| `browser_mode` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_AUTH_BROWSER_MODE:-auto}"` | Which interactive sign-in flow every backend uses. One setting for the whole run, so that --headless means the same thing for every credential. Every sign-in ends with a code pasted back by default, display or not. The alternative, a loopback redirect, hands the result to a listener on localhost -- and nothing here can check beforehand that the browser will get back there: which machine the page ends up on, an organisation's sign-in page or browser policy that stops it returning to http://localhost, a port in use. A display proves only that a browser can be drawn. When the redirect does not arrive, the sign-in waits with nothing to paste. The code works wherever signing in works. auto      take a pasted code; where a browser can be shown, the URL is opened in it for you (auth.signin.open_url). headless  take a pasted code and open nothing: you carry the URL to any browser, on any machine. --headless. browser   the loopback redirect, for a browser known to reach this machine. --browser-loopback-redirect. The two flags are alternatives; giving both is refused rather than letting the later one quietly win. |
| `force` | `false` | Re-authenticate even when detection already found a valid credential. --force-auth is the command-line form of setting this to true. Detection runs either way: what this changes is whether the result is acted on. |
| `reset` | `false` | Throw the existing credential away before signing in again. --force-auth-with-reset is the command-line form, and it sets `force` too. Why this is not simply what --force-auth does: forcing a sign-in *adds* a fresh credential and can be repeated all day, while clearing one takes a credential away from the whole machine -- `gcloud auth revoke` logs out every tool on the host that reads that account, not only Claude Code. The two are different promises, so they are different flags, and this one is the longer thing to type. It is also what to reach for when --force-auth "did not ask me anything": gcloud and claude.ai both re-use a session the provider still holds, so the browser rubber-stamps the login without a password. Clearing the credential first is what makes the sign-in a real one. Note that the provider's own cookie lives in the browser, not here -- see auth.reset_browser_profile. Guarded three ways: it never runs without being asked for by name, it asks for confirmation first (--auto-agree answers yes, a non-interactive session answers no), and --dry-run reports what it would remove without removing it. |
| `reset_backup` | `false` | Move credential files aside as <name>.<timestamp>.bak instead of deleting them. Off, unlike the settings.json writer's own backups, because a backup of a credential is still a credential: leaving a readable copy beside the file somebody just asked to have cleared defeats the request. Turn it on if you would rather have the way back than the clean slate. |
| `reset_backup_suffix` | `"%Y%m%d-%H%M%S"` |  |
| `reset_timeout_seconds` | `120` | Seconds allowed for one revoke/logout command. These are quick, or broken. |
| `reset_browser_profile` | `true` | Also delete the browser profile this program keeps under its state directory, so the sign-in that follows starts with no cookie for the provider -- which is the difference between being asked who you are and being waved through. Only this program's own profile is touched: your everyday browser profile is yours, and clearing it would sign you out of everything else you have open. A reset also turns auth.browser.clean_profile from 'auto' into 'always', because a freshly emptied profile is no use if the sign-in does not open it. A pasted-code sign-in (--headless) opens no browser at all -- you carry the URL yourself -- so the emptied profile is not used by itself, and a browser you paste the URL into that is still signed in would wave you through. So after a reset the URL handed over signs that browser out first, where the provider allows it (auth.signin.sign_out_first); otherwise you are told, and given commands to run for a sign-in that asks: this profile, a private window, or signing out first. See auth.signin.open_url to have the URL opened for you instead. |
| `interactive_timeout_seconds` | `1800` | Seconds to wait for a human to complete an interactive login. Generous on purpose: this is a person moving a URL to another machine, signing in, maybe passing 2FA, and carrying a code back. Expiring mid-flow kills gcloud while the browser still says "success", which reads exactly like a hang. 0 waits for as long as it takes. |
| `live_probe` | `true` | Spend a token on a real round-trip to prove the credential works. Disable in CI to avoid the cost; presence checks still run. |

### `[auth.signin]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `pty` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_AUTH_SIGNIN_PTY:-auto}"` | Sit between the terminal and the sign-in so its output can be read. auto    whenever there is a terminal to sit in the middle of always  / never -- `never` hands the terminal straight to the child, as before, and nothing is captured. |
| `columns` | `0` | Size of the pseudo-terminal the sign-in sees. 0 means "the same as this terminal", which is what keeps its output looking the way it was designed to. Setting columns very wide stops a child that hard-wraps from breaking the URL on screen, at the cost of every box it draws being that wide too. |
| `rows` | `0` |  |
| `url_pattern` | `"https://\\S{60,}"` | What counts as the sign-in URL in that stream. Deliberately demanding: a short link in a banner or a docs URL in a warning is not what anyone is waiting for. |
| `deliver` | `["file", "clipboard"]` | Where to put it, in order; every one that works is used. Both are silent -- the child owns the screen while it is waiting. file       write it to paths.state_dir/url_file, private, removed afterwards clipboard  pipe it to the first tool below that is installed |
| `url_file` | `"sign-in-url.txt"` |  |
| `clipboard_timeout_seconds` | `10` | How long a clipboard tool may take to take the copy. |
| `open_url` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_AUTH_SIGNIN_OPEN_URL:-auto}"` | Open the captured URL in the browser found for this run (auth.browser; this program's own profile when it keeps one). It needs a display, a browser, and the capture (pty). You sign in there and paste the code the page shows back. Anything else, including "reset" (once the default, and the cause of a browser opening under --headless after --force-auth-with-reset), means never. auto    unless --headless (auth.browser_mode = headless), which means you open the URL yourself always  every pasted-code sign-in, --headless included never   leave opening the URL to you |
| `open_settle_seconds` | `2` | Seconds to watch that browser for an immediate failure before going back to the sign-in. It keeps running either way; this only decides what is logged. |
| `sign_out_first` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_AUTH_SIGNIN_SIGN_OUT_FIRST:-reset}"` | Whether the URL a pasted-code sign-in hands over first goes through the provider's sign-out page, which then continues to the sign-in. Every copy you can reach is that URL: the file, the clipboard, and the one on screen, which is repainted as it passes through this program's terminal proxy. The browser you paste it into is out of this program's reach, so a reset alone leaves it signed in, and it lets you through with no password. The provider's own sign-out is the one thing that reaches it, wherever it is. Needs auth.<backend>.signout_url and signout_continue_param, and the capture (auth.signin.pty); without the capture the sign-in's own URL is shown as is. reset   after --force-auth-with-reset always  every pasted-code sign-in never   hand over the sign-in URL unchanged |
| `idp_signout_url` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_AUTH_SIGNIN_IDP_SIGNOUT_URL:-}"` | Your organisation's sign-out page, for an account that signs in through the organisation's own sign-in page (single sign-on). The provider's sign-out ends only the provider's session; that page keeps its own, on its own site, and signs you straight back in with no password. Set, it is the first stop of the URL handed over whenever sign_out_first applies: {continue} is replaced with the rest of the chain, URL-encoded, so the page must be willing to continue there (most identity providers want that address allowed first). There is no default: every organisation's page is its own. A private window clears it too, with nothing to configure. e.g. https://<your-sign-in-host>/<sign-out-path>?<its-continue-param>={continue} |

### `[auth.browser]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `command` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_AUTH_BROWSER:-${BROWSER:-}}"` | A command to use verbatim, with %s standing in for the URL -- the same shape the BROWSER variable has always had, so an operator who already knows that convention knows this one. --browser. Empty means "find one below", which is the ordinary case. |
| `candidates` | `[ …` | Binaries that count as a browser, in preference order. Firefox leads because it is packaged by every distribution in this program's reach, ships the same build to all of them, and needs no sandbox concession to run as root -- the three things that decide whether a sign-in page renders at all on the hosts this runs on. xdg-open is deliberately absent: it is a launcher, not a browser, and on a machine with nothing registered it succeeds at opening nothing. It appears under `openers` instead, where its real role is. |
| `openers` | `["wslview", "xdg-open", "gio", "open"]` | Tried when no candidate is on PATH. These reach a browser this side of the machine cannot see: the Windows half of a WSL install, a flatpak the host registered, a desktop handler with no binary of its own. |
| `openers_reading_browser_variable` | `["xdg-open", "gio"]` | Openers that consult BROWSER themselves. Naming one of these in BROWSER makes it call itself for ever, so when the search falls through to one of them the variable is left alone and the opener is used as the host intended. wslview is absent, which is why exporting it works and is the standard WSL recipe. |
| `set_browser_variable` | `true` | Export BROWSER so gcloud and the claude CLI open the browser chosen here rather than each guessing separately. An operator who has already exported BROWSER is left alone -- the interpolation above adopts their value. |
| `clean_profile` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_AUTH_BROWSER_PROFILE:-auto}"` | Sign in in a profile belonging to this program rather than the operator's own. auto     only where the default profile is unlikely to be usable: no desktop session, or running as root. always   /  never A dedicated profile has no extension filtering the sign-in form and no other Google account already signed in -- the "it opened in the wrong profile" failure that --headless is usually reached for as a workaround. |
| `input_method_fix` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_AUTH_BROWSER_IM_FIX:-auto}"` | Make typed text actually reach the page. auto     only where the failure is possible: an X display with no desktop session behind it, and no input method configured. always   apply it regardless. Reach for this if the sign-in form loses what you type -- it is the single most likely cure. never    leave the toolkit environment exactly as found. Correct on a desktop running ibus, fcitx or any other real input method, where overriding it would break composing non-Latin text. |

### `[auth.google_cloud]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `method` | `"auto"` | How to acquire the credential: user               interactive `gcloud auth login` service-account    activate the key file named by service_account_key_ref impersonate        act as impersonate_service_account, from your own credential adc-only           application-default login, without a CLI login workload-identity  an external account config is already in place metadata           the GCE/GKE metadata server already provides one auto               pick from what is configured and what the host looks like |
| `account` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_GCP_ACCOUNT:-${GOOGLE_CLOUD_USER_ACCOUNT:-}}"` | Account to make active, as --gcloud-user-account. Empty means "keep whatever gcloud already has"; when set, an active account that differs counts as unauthenticated, so phase 2 signs in rather than proceeding as the wrong user. |
| `project` | `"${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT:-${CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT:-${ANTHROPIC_VERTE…` | The project this run is for, as --gcloud-project (--vertex-project), which sets provision.vertex.project to the same value: one project, named once, for both the sign-in and what gets provisioned afterwards. Signing in is not project-neutral -- quota, API enablement and Vertex model access are all charged to a project -- so when this is set every gcloud command below carries it (see project_args) and gcloud's own active project is pointed at it. |
| `configure_adc` | `true` | Application Default Credentials are what the Vertex AI SDK actually reads. |
| `service_account_key_ref` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_GCP_SA_KEY_REF:-}"` | Reference to a service-account key file, as --gcloud-service-account-file. Never the key itself: gcloud opens the file, the contents never pass through this process. Setting it selects the 'service-account' method, which wins the tie-break against the impersonation below -- so the two are alternatives, and giving both on the command line is refused rather than silently resolved. |
| `impersonate_service_account` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_GCP_IMPERSONATE:-}"` | Impersonate a service account using the logged-in user's credentials, as --gcloud-service-account. Setting it selects the 'impersonate' method, and an already-authenticated host that is not impersonating it is re-authenticated. An identity, not a credential: the key never leaves Google. |
| `impersonate_adc` | `true` | gcloud's config impersonation reaches the gcloud CLI only; Claude Code reads the application-default credential.  With this on, that credential is written impersonating the account too (commands.adc_impersonate, an interactive sign-in), unless it already does -- read from adc_file's type and impersonation URL, never its tokens. |
| `adc_file` | `"${CLOUDSDK_CONFIG:-${HOME}/.config/gcloud}/application_default_cre…` |  |
| `quota_project` | `""` |  |
| `required_apis` | `["aiplatform.googleapis.com"]` | APIs phase 3 needs; checked (not enabled) unless enable_apis is true. |
| `enable_apis` | `false` |  |
| `signout_url` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_GCP_SIGNOUT_URL:-https://accounts.google.co…` | Where to sign out of the provider in a browser. The reset revokes this machine's credential, but only this page ends the browser's session. Empty offers none. |
| `signout_continue_param` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_GCP_SIGNOUT_CONTINUE_PARAM:-continue}"` | The query parameter signout_url follows once the browser is signed out. With it, a pasted-code sign-in after a reset hands over signout_url?<param>=<the sign-in URL>: whichever browser it is pasted into is signed out of Google first (every account in it), then lands on the sign-in (with reset_prompt below; an organisation's own sign-in page needs auth.signin.idp_signout_url). Google follows it only to its own sign-in host, which is also the only host it is used for. See auth.signin.sign_out_first. Empty turns the chaining off and leaves the advice. |
| `reset_prompt` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_GCP_RESET_PROMPT:-select_account}"` | prompt values added to the sign-in behind that sign-out (space-separated; those already there are kept). Signing out does not make Google forget the accounts used in that browser, and it may carry on with one of them unasked -- straight to an organisation's sign-in page, for a single sign-on account. select_account shows the account chooser instead, with "Use another account" to type an email. Empty adds nothing. |
| `project_args` | `["--project", "{project}"]` | Appended to every command below when project is set, so the sign-in, the tokens it mints and the API checks all happen against the named project rather than whichever one gcloud was last pointed at. --project is a gcloud-wide flag accepted by every command, and it beats CLOUDSDK_CORE_PROJECT and the active configuration for that one invocation. Set it to [] to leave gcloud's own project resolution alone. |
| `project_args_skip` | `[ …` | Commands that must not get it: the two that set the project take it as their argument, and the two that read one would otherwise be handed the answer and echo it straight back -- which would hide the fact that gcloud's own project is unset or different, and that is exactly what phase 2 is checking. |
| `unset_values` | `["(unset)", "None"]` | What `gcloud config get-value` prints for a property that is not set. Read as "no value" by every caller, so a missing project is never taken for a project called "(unset)". |

## 30-provision

Source: [`initialize_claude_ai/data/30-provision.toml`](../initialize_claude_ai/data/30-provision.toml)

### `[provision]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `backend` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_BACKEND:-auto}"` | vertex \| anthropic-api \| bedrock \| auto 'auto' picks the first backend that phase 2 actually authenticated, following backend_priority below. |
| `backend_priority` | `["vertex", "anthropic-api", "bedrock"]` |  |
| `merge_settings` | `true` | Merge into the existing settings.json instead of replacing it. |
| `backup_settings` | `true` | Keep a timestamped copy before every write. |
| `backup_suffix` | `"%Y%m%d-%H%M%S"` |  |
| `scope` | `"user"` | Write settings at user scope (~/.claude/settings.json) or project scope. |
| `export_env` | `true` | Also write the discovered values into the initialize-claude-ai env files. |
| `retire_stale_env` | `true` | Take out of settings.json (and the env files) the variables this phase wrote for a backend that is no longer the selected one. Merging alone cannot delete, so without this, provisioning anthropic-api over a machine that previously ran Vertex leaves CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX = "1" behind and Claude Code keeps routing to Vertex -- from a file nobody remembers editing. Only names this phase is capable of writing are ever removed: the union of every backend's [env] keys and [env_names] values. A variable the operator put in settings.json themselves is outside that set and is never touched. Set false to make phase 3 purely additive again. |
| `discover_models` | `true` | Query the provider for the live model list rather than trusting the catalog. |
| `model_discovery_timeout_seconds` | `30` |  |
| `strict_model_check` | `false` | Fail the phase when the configured model is not offered by the backend. |
| `overwrite_inferred_model` | `false` | Replace a model already present in settings.json even when initialize-claude-ai only inferred one. Off: an explicit choice such as "opus" survives a re-run, and --default-model (or provision.settings.model) still overrides it. |
| `overwrite_existing_settings` | `false` | The same rule for the other non-env keys under [provision.settings] below -- theme, tui, permissions.defaultMode. Off, they are seeded when settings.json does not answer the question yet and left alone when it does, because Claude Code writes that file too: /theme and /permissions put the operator's own answer there, and a re-run of phase 3 has no business undoing it. Set true to make the configured values authoritative on every run. |
| `require_model` | `true` | Stop the phase when no tier resolved to a model at all. There is nothing reasonable left to write at that point: Claude Code would be pointed at a backend with no model to call it with. |
| `tiers` | `["opus", "sonnet", "haiku"]` | Model tiers Claude Code understands, largest first. |
| `default_tier` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_DEFAULT_TIER:-opus}"` | Which of those tiers Claude Code opens on when --default-model says nothing. settings.json "model" is written as the tier name itself -- "opus" -- so this is literally the value that lands there; the id it resolved to goes into ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_OPUS_MODEL instead, where a tier switch inside Claude Code still finds it. |
| `settings_filename` | `"settings.json"` | Settings file names, relative to the chosen scope's directory. |
| `project_settings_dir` | `".claude"` |  |
| `project_local_settings_filename` | `"settings.local.json"` | Where a credential goes when scope = "project": .claude/settings.json is the file Claude Code means to be committed, so a credential (and every value kept out of .mcp.json) goes to the project's local settings file instead, which Claude Code reads the same way and keeps out of version control.  With scope = "user" it goes to the user's settings.json, as everything else does. |

### `[provision.settings]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `model` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MODEL:-${DEFAULT_MODEL:-}}"` | Non-env keys written into settings.json, alongside the env block. Every key in this section (and in the sub-tables below) is written as it stands, so adding one here is all it takes to have phase 3 write it -- no code change. Empty values are dropped, which is also how a key is switched off, by the setting rather than by the variable below it -- `--set provision.settings.tui=` or INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_PROVISION__SETTINGS__TUI= . (Blanking the short variable does not: an empty environment variable means "unset" everywhere here, which is what makes the defaults below defaults at all.) Except for model, these are seeded rather than enforced: see provision.overwrite_existing_settings above. Which model Claude Code opens on, as a tier name -- opus, sonnet, haiku -- rather than an id. --default-model. A tier keeps working when the models move on, and keeps settings.json portable: the backends spell the same model three different ways, and the id the selected one wants is exported as ANTHROPIC_DEFAULT_<TIER>_MODEL. Given an id here, phase 3 writes the tier that id belongs to. Left empty, provision.default_tier decides. |
| `theme` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_THEME:-auto}"` | Colour scheme: auto follows the terminal's own light/dark setting, which is the only one that is right on a machine whose terminal theme is not known here. |
| `tui` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_TUI:-fullscreen}"` | Terminal layout. fullscreen gives Claude Code the alternate screen buffer. |

### `[provision.vertex]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_USE_VERTEX:-${CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX:-1}}"` | Whether this host may be provisioned against Vertex at all. --use-vertex. 1, the default, leaves it first in backend_priority, so `backend = "auto"` picks it as soon as Google Cloud is authenticated. 0 takes it out of that walk entirely, and turns `--provision-backend vertex` into a refusal rather than a silent fall-through to another provider. |
| `enable_flag` | `"--use-vertex 1"` | Named in the remediation when this backend is asked for while switched off, so the message points at the flag rather than at a config key. |
| `project` | `"${ANTHROPIC_VERTEX_PROJECT_ID:-${GOOGLE_CLOUD_PROJECT:-${CLOUDSDK_…` | The project Vertex calls are billed to. --gcloud-project (or --vertex-project, the same flag). No project id is invented here: a wrong one bills somebody else and fails with a permission error naming a project the operator never chose. Phase 3 resolves it from this setting, then from the project phase 2 actually signed in against, then from gcloud's active project -- so a host that authenticated already has one. |
| `region` | `"${CLOUD_ML_REGION:-${GOOGLE_CLOUD_LOCATION:-global}}"` | --gcloud-region. 'global', 'us' and 'europe' are multi-region locations; single regions such as us-east5 also work and get their own endpoint host. 'global' is the default because it is the location reachable without knowing anything about where the project's quota lives. |
| `known_regions` | `[ …` |  |
| `publisher` | `"anthropic"` |  |
| `endpoint_template` | `"https://{region}-aiplatform.googleapis.com"` | {region} and {project} are substituted at run time. |
| `global_endpoint_template` | `"https://aiplatform.googleapis.com"` |  |
| `global_regions` | `["global", "us", "europe"]` | Locations that have no host of their own and are served by the global one. Verified live: us-east5-aiplatform.googleapis.com answers, but us-aiplatform.googleapis.com 404s every route -- 'us' and 'europe' are multi-region *locations*, not regional endpoints. |
| `fallback_to_global_catalogue` | `true` | If the regional host has no publisher catalogue, ask the global host instead rather than reporting the region as offering no models. |
| `models_path_template` | `"/v1beta1/publishers/{publisher}/models"` | Verified live: the publisher-model catalogue is only served on v1beta1; the v1 route returns 404. Response shape: {"publisherModels": [...], "nextPageToken"?}. |
| `models_page_size` | `200` |  |
| `max_pages` | `10` | Stop after this many pages even if the catalogue keeps offering a next token, so a paginating endpoint that never terminates cannot hang the phase. |
| `quota_project` | `"${GOOGLE_CLOUD_QUOTA_PROJECT:-}"` | Sent as x-goog-user-project so the call is billed/quota'd to the right project. |
| `default_model` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_VERTEX_MODEL:-}"` | Model ids to write into settings. Vertex uses name@version. |
| `token_refs` | `["gcloud-adc", "gcloud-token"]` | Credential references used to call the model catalogue. First hit wins. |
| `login_env` | `["GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS"]` | Variables Claude Code reads to log in that phase 2 may set (a service-account key's path).  Written into settings.json's env block when set -- never only into env.sh, which a new terminal does not source -- and never when the value is shaped like a credential. |
| `accepted_launch_stages` | `["GA", "PUBLIC_PREVIEW"]` | Only offer models whose launchStage is in this list. Empty = accept all. |
| `model_version_separator` | `"@"` | Vertex model ids carry a version suffix: claude-sonnet-4-5@20250929. |
| `placeholder_versions` | `["default", "latest"]` | versionId values that are placeholders rather than a dated release. Verified live: the newest models report versionId "default", and 'claude-opus-5@default' is not an address the backend accepts -- they are used by bare id. |

## 40-mcp

Source: [`initialize_claude_ai/data/40-mcp.toml`](../initialize_claude_ai/data/40-mcp.toml)

### `[mcp]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `agentic` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_AGENTIC:-true}"` | Let each stage start as a Claude subagent (--no-agent sets this false). False runs the deterministic pipeline directly: no runtime is looked for, no workspace is made and no turn is spent, so the phase is repeatable and costs nothing -- at the price of the reasoning that finds a server whose endpoint is not where convention would put it. Whichever this is, every stage line and the phase banner say which mode was used; nothing about it is silent. |
| `servers` | `[]` | Servers to discover against: full URLs, bare domains or host:port, in any mixture. Each one is canonicalised before use -- see [mcp.address]. Normally supplied with --mcp-server; this is the persistent default. |
| `exhaustive` | `false` | Record every working endpoint found for an address instead of stopping at the first one (--exhaustive-mcp).  Every stage runs and every candidate path is probed, and each endpoint that completes a handshake is registered. |
| `pick_best` | `false` | Keep only the best server found for each address instead of registering every one that answers (--the-best-mcp).  Turning this on widens the search first -- there is no "best of" without alternatives -- so a run takes longer.  How "best" is decided is entirely in [mcp.ranking]. |
| `recheck` | `false` | Prove the addresses again after the operator acted on the report (--mcp-recheck): only their existing registrations and the last working entry ([mcp.known_good]) are tried, with the usage contract and the repairs; nothing is searched for.  Seconds, not a discovery run. |
| `recheck_all_word` | `"all"` | `--mcp-recheck all` re-checks every entry of the project file: the address each serves is the one its last proof recorded ([mcp.known_good]), else the host whose name the entry carries (name == the host with dashes for dots, as this program names entries).  An entry neither ties to an address is named, never guessed at.  What it is for: a .mcp.json copied from another machine, proved on this one -- its paths, its start-up time against Claude Code's wait, and where its credentials are kept -- without typing every address. |
| `stages` | `["endpoint", "package", "bridge", "strategy"]` | Stages to run, in order. |
| `register_scope` | `"local"` | local \| user \| project -- passed to `claude mcp add --scope`. |
| `name_prefix` | `""` | Prefix for generated server names.  The base name is always the target's full FQDN with dashes for dots (mcp.example.com -> mcp-example-com); when one address yields several endpoints, each name also carries a suffix saying which endpoint it is. |
| `mcp_json_path` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_JSON:-.mcp.json}"` | Where the discovered servers are written.  Every verified server is always written here AND registered with the CLI; there is no switch for either. Relative, so it lands in the directory the command was run from -- which is exactly where Claude Code looks for a project's MCP servers, so the file works where it is written instead of having to be found first.  Give an absolute path here (or in INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_JSON) to put it somewhere else. |

### `[mcp.policy]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `agent_claims_close_tiers` | `false` | What an agent's report says it found (native endpoints, endpoints behind a login) is a claim: recorded and reported, never allowed to close the lower tiers -- only an endpoint a probe here showed to speak MCP does. confluence.example.com's /mcp, which redirects to the login page like every path that does not exist, was reported "behind authentication" and closed the package, bridge and strategy stages; mcp-atlassian was never tried. |
| `native_first` | `true` | Enforce the tier order at all.  Off: every stage runs as it likes, which is the pre-policy behaviour and is not recommended. |
| `require_checklist` | `true` | Refuse tiers 2-3 while the checklist has unperformed steps. |
| `forbid_lower_tiers_when_native` | `true` | Refuse tiers 2-3 outright once a native endpoint has been found. |
| `lower_tiers_when_wall_is_foreign` | `true` | ...except when the only thing tier 1 found is a credential wall on a host that belongs to neither the target nor its organisation, and nothing there ever completed a handshake.  Then "tier 1 exists" is a hypothesis, and it is being used to forbid the tiers that could test it. confluence.example.com is why.  Tier 1 answered https://mcp.atlassian.com/v2/mcp -- Atlassian Cloud's multi-tenant endpoint, which serves `*.atlassian.net` tenants, not a customer's self-hosted Data Center wiki, as the same stage's own step D had already concluded from the SSO redirect.  That one URL shut tiers 2, 3 and 4, so `mcp-atlassian` -- which does talk to Data Center, given CONFLUENCE_URL and a PAT -- was never looked for.  The one target with a real tier-2 answer got the only wrong tier-1. A proven endpoint still closes the lower tiers wherever it lives: api.githubcopilot.com serving github.com is the ordinary shape of a hosted offering.  What no longer closes them is an unproven address on someone else's domain.  Setting this false restores the older behaviour. |
| `native_must_be_registrable` | `true` | Only an endpoint that could actually be registered for the target counts as "tier 1 exists".  One that answered MCP but that the registration check refuses -- found by a keyword search and tied to nothing -- is retracted from the checklist with its reason (reported under `ruled_out`), and closes no tier. confluence.example.com is why, a second time.  The registry returned mcp.0dteconfluence.com for "confluence" -- an options-trading server; the word is a trading term.  It handshaked with 37 tools, was recorded as the native endpoint, and shut the package, bridge and strategy stages; the registration check refused it seconds later and the address ended with nothing. false: every endpoint that answered is recorded, as before. |
| `vet_record_before_gate` | `true` | Probe, after every stage, any endpoint the checklist believes in that no judged candidate backs -- most often one an agent named in its checklist without offering it as a candidate -- so the next gate reads only endpoints that could be written down.  false: they are tested only by the final reconcile, after the stages they closed were already skipped. |
| `reopen_when_native_retracted` | `true` | The last safety net: if a stage was refused because of a native endpoint that was later ruled out, run that stage after all (agent first, in agentic mode). |
| `mandatory_paths` | `[ …` | Step A's proof.  Every one of these must have been probed before step A counts as done; they are the non-traditional subpaths that are missed by stopping at /mcp.  Add to this list for a vendor with its own convention. |

|---|---|---|

| `package` | `2` |  |
| `bridge` | `3` |  |
| `strategy` | `3` |  |

### `[mcp.instructions]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `replacement_tools_shown` | `8` | When an entry replaces an earlier one of the same name with a different server, the briefing names this many of its tools, and of the tools the earlier one offered -- jira_get_issue became get_request on sd.example.com. |
| `enabled` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_BRIEFING:-true}"` | Print the briefing and keep it in the log.  Turning this off silences the screen; the JSON report still carries it, so nothing is lost, only quieter. |
| `strip_keys` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_STRIP_KEYS:-_instructions}"` | Top-level keys in an existing .mcp.json that this program wrote in an earlier version and now removes on sight, so a file carried over from one gets clean. Swept at the start of every phase-4 run and again whenever the file is written, because a run that discovers nothing still leaves a file somebody may copy today.  Only names listed here are touched: any other top-level key is the operator's. |
| `warn_on_duplicates` | `true` | Compare new entries against the ones already in the file and warn when two point at the same host -- the usual way a .mcp.json quietly grows duplicates. |

### `[mcp.verification.advertised]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `entries` | `200` |  |
| `value_chars` | `400` |  |
| `schema_depth` | `4` |  |
| `schema_list_items` | `40` | How many items of a JSON array to walk before stopping. |
| `instruction_chars` | `2000` | Characters kept of `instructions`, which is prose and can be long. |
| `describing_keys` | `["uri", "uriTemplate", "description", "title"]` | Keys in a tools/resources/prompts listing entry whose value is the server's own words or the server's own address, rather than a name we supplied.  `uri` is the single best one: an Open Build Service server lists https://build.opensuse.org/... there, and nothing else in the exchange says that as plainly -- while `name` is often just a label and was, for a long time, the only field kept. |
| `schema_keys` | `["description", "default", "const", "title", "pattern", "format"]` | ...and the keys inside a JSON Schema that carry prose or a value the server chose.  A generic server is configured through exactly these: a `base_url` whose `default` is the target is the server saying what it serves. |
| `schema_containers` | `["inputSchema", "arguments"]` | Where in a listing entry a JSON Schema is found.  `inputSchema` is the tools spelling and `arguments` the prompts one. |

### `[mcp.env_contract]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `launcher_names` | `[ …` | What runs a server is never the server, binary or not: matched whole against a launched file's name (and its symlink target's).  Homebrew's npx is a JavaScript file; its own process.env[key] was read as the server's, and gitlab-example-net's HEADERS slot was "renamed" to key. |
| `read_packages` | `true` | Also read the variables a *package* reads, from its installed source, so a credential under a name the package never reads is caught before it is trusted: build.example.net's entry put its login in BUILD_EXAMPLE_NET_BASE64_OF_USER_PASSWORD, which mcp-openapi-proxy never reads (it reads API_KEY and EXTRA_HEADERS).  Only an installed copy is read -- nothing is downloaded for this -- and at most max_package_files files of it. |
| `max_package_files` | `400` |  |
| `max_bytes` | `2000000` | Files larger than this are not scanned (bytes).  Binaries never are. |
| `default_window_lines` | `6` | How many lines after a read to look for the file its fallback opens: path = os.environ.get("X") or os.path.join(HERE, "ops.json") Only a quoted name that exists beside the script counts. |
| `fallback_literal_patterns` | `[ …` | A read with no default of its own that falls back to a literal right after it -- os.environ.get("X") or "30", process.env.X \|\| "30", also on the next line -- has that literal as its default.  Matched against what follows the read (the same default_window_lines), each with a `default` group.  The generated gitlab.example.net bridge read MCP_BRIDGE_USER_AGENT this way; with its default unseen, a value equal to it was taken for a credential. |
| `constant_patterns` | `[ …` | A variable read through a constant naming it -- TOKEN_VAR = "GITLAB_EXAMPLE_NET_TOKEN" then os.environ[TOKEN_VAR]: constant_patterns bind a name to a literal (groups `const` and `value`), indirect_read_patterns read through it (group `ref`). gitlab-example-net's bridge read its token so, and was called "never read". |
| `indirect_read_patterns` | `[ …` |  |
| `read_patterns` | `[ …` | One regex per idiom, each with a `name` group (or `name2`) and an optional `default` group.  Add a line to teach it another language. |
| `package_read_patterns` | `[ …` | The same idioms for a package's installed source, without the shell one: in JavaScript ${X} is a template literal, not a read. |
| `credential_in_default` | `'''://[^/@\s:]+:[^/@\s]+@'''` | A default found in the source is copied into the entry -- unless it is, or carries, a credential.  Secret-named variables and values that look like a token are caught by the shared secret policy; this catches a password inside a URL (https://user:pw@host) under an innocent name.  Such a read is written ${NAME:-} instead. |
| `session_variables` | `[ …` | Variables the operator's login session sets (an SSH agent's socket, a Kerberos cache).  A script that reads one gets it under its own name as ${NAME:-} -- never renamed per server (BUILD_EXAMPLE_NET_SSH_AUTH_SOCK is a name nobody has), never treated as a credential, never listed as something to export; an existing entry that renamed or pinned one is written back this way. |
| `ignore` | `[ …` | Variables that describe the host rather than configure the server.  Writing HOME into an entry would pin this machine's home into every copy.  The trust variables are [mcp.trust]'s to write, and the names in [mcp.verification.client_env] passthrough are handed over by the client already. |

### `[mcp.launch_form]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | A launcher is not the program, and installed is not runnable.  An installer's private launcher -- a `uv tool` or pipx environment's script, an npm global module's bin -- runs only beside its own install: bugzilla-opensuse-org was written to run .../uv/tools/mcp-bugzilla/bin/mcp-bugzilla, a script whose first line runs that tool's own Python; copied to another machine it could not start (no such file), and pointed at the system's Python it could not import mcp_bugzilla.  Such a command is launched by its portable form (the package, pinned to the version installed, through uvx / npx) on every path: before each trial (what is trialled is what is written), in the final check of .mcp.json (repair_in_file) and in phase 1 (install.portable_launchers). A command is runnable only when it exists, is executable, the interpreter its first line names exists, and -- import_check -- a Python launcher's interpreter can import the module it starts. |
| `repair_in_file` | `true` |  |
| `import_check` | `true` |  |
| `import_check_timeout_seconds` | `15` |  |

| `pin` | `"@{version}"` |  |
| `metadata` | `"node"` |  |
| `installers` | `["npm", "pnpm", "yarn"]` |  |

### `[mcp.healing]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | Repair an entry that does not start.  false turns off the repairs only: the entry is still launched as written and its verdict still counts. |
| `agent_first` | `true` | Ask the agent before trying the rules.  false runs the rules first and asks the agent only if they all fail -- cheaper, and worse at anything the rules were not written for. |
| `agent_enabled` | `true` | Let the agent repair at all.  false leaves the deterministic repairs, which is also what a --no-agent run gets. |
| `repairs` | `[ …` | The deterministic repairs, in order.  Each is one known difference between our launch and the client's: declare_inherited_env  a variable our trial inherited from the operator's shell and the entry never declared.  The commonest by far, and the reason `starts` used to disagree with Claude Code. absolute_command       a bare command resolved through *our* PATH. absolute_args          a relative path, resolved against the directory the candidate was trialled in. withdraw_optional_reads  the ${NAME:-} slots [mcp.env_contract] writes for a variable the script reads and nobody set, for the rare server that treats "set but empty" unlike "unset". isolate_user_config    the server reads the operator's own configuration (a dotfile under HOME or XDG_CONFIG_HOME) and that configuration breaks it: the entry gets a config scope of its own -- see [mcp.healing.isolation]. restore_path_defaults  the entry names one of this program's own path variables (mcp.registration.path_variables, interpreter_variable, launcher variables) without its ${NAME:-default}, so nothing resolves it. drop_unset_setting     a setting (not a credential) holds a ${NAME} nothing sets, and Claude Code passes it as literal text: bugzilla-opensuse-org exited on "--bugzilla-auth-mode '${BUGZILLA_AUTH_MODE}'".  The setting is left out, so the server's default applies. Empty turns the deterministic half off. |
| `keep_credential_slots` | `true` | A repair never withdraws a credential slot (a declared credential, a secret name, an adapter's credential_env key): it is the only place the login can go, and an entry starts without it only because nobody logs in. gitlab-example-net lost HEADERS to withdraw_optional_reads and every call went out as anybody.  A slot the server takes in a form is rewritten in that form instead -- see [mcp.discovery.reuse] credential_in_taken_form. |
| `report_files` | `true` | When an entry cannot be made to start, list the host files it depends on with their size and age. A bridge is a script plus the data it reads, and the commonest way one breaks is that something regenerated half of it.  The evidence is right there in the filesystem -- a script modified today beside a manifest from yesterday -- and nobody looks, because nothing says to look.  openqa.example.net broke that way twice: first as `AttributeError: 'list' object has no attribute 'items'`, then, once the pair carried a stamp, as an honest refusal -- and in both cases the fact that settled it was two timestamps a day apart. |
| `files_agree_within_seconds` | `3600` | Files written further apart than this are called out as probably-stale rather than merely listed.  An hour is generous for a pair written by one run. |
| `report_differences` | `true` | ...and say how the launch that was proven differs from the entry as a client runs it: variables the trial set or inherited (names of those naming a file) that the entry does not declare, and the directory each ran from.  Names only, never values.  confluence.example.com's entry died with a FileNotFoundError that named no file, and nothing said which side of that gap held it. |
| `examine_pending` | `true` | A server waiting for a credential settles its target just as a working one does, so its entry must start too before it may -- examined in the stage, with the stand-in credential its trial used filling the slot.  Without this, confluence.example.com's two such candidates were never launched as written until publish, where the one chosen failed and nothing else was tried. |

| `directory` | `"${cfg:mcp.agent.workspace}/artifacts/isolated-config/{slug}"` |  |

### `[mcp.trust]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `bundle` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_TRUST_BUNDLE:-}"` | Pin a bundle, or leave empty to take the first candidate that exists. |
| `bundle_candidates` | `[ …` | Where distributions keep the system bundle.  An empty list turns detection off, for a host where naming the bundle is the wrong thing to do. |
| `extra_ca` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_TRUST_EXTRA_CA:-}"` | Everything below is additive: it adds authorities to what this program's own requests trust and to what the servers it registers are told about, and never removes one or turns verification off.  See core/trust_store.py. The operator's own authorities, as PEM files (comma-separated).  The supported way to reach a target behind an internal CA this host does not hold.  --mcp-trust-ca FILE[,FILE]. |
| `include_certifi` | `true` | Add certifi's bundle, when it is installed, to what this program trusts. httpx used to trust certifi alone and the urllib fallback the host alone; both now trust both. |
| `partial_chain` | `true` | Let a certificate in the trust store end a chain even when it is not a self-signed root.  A server that sends "intermediate, then a CA issued by a root it does not send" can then be verified by trusting what it does send. Python 3.13 sets this by default; older ones and generated bridges get it here. |
| `complete_to_root` | `true` | ...but a file handed to a server is read by *its* runtime, and Node accepts no partial chain: the run's bundle carried smelt.example.net's chain only to a cross-signed "Example CA Root", and a Node server failed every request with it. So a chain that falls short is completed up to a self-signed root from the issuers this machine already has -- the host's store, --mcp-trust-ca, the anchor folders below and the CA files MCP entries here already name -- and kept only when it then verifies strictly. |
| `issuer_sources` | `["/usr/share/pki/trust/anchors/*", "/etc/pki/trust/anchors/*", "/et…` |  |
| `issuers_from_entries` | `true` |  |
| `issuers_from_program_dirs` | `true` | ...and the copies this program keeps: known-good file copies and the servers' own folders (mcp.registration.artifacts_home).  A root found is then kept in the anchors folder, so it outlives the file it came from. |
| `max_chain_depth` | `6` |  |
| `expiry_warning_days` | `60` | A certificate on a target's chain that expires within this many days is named in the report: every entry reaching that host stops working then. 0 = never. |
| `pin_presented_chain` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_TRUST_PIN_PRESENTED_CHAIN:-targets}"` | When an address given with --mcp-server presents a certificate from an authority nothing here trusts: targets  learn the chain it presents (never its own certificate), keep it under store_dir, and trust it for this and later runs -- trust on first use, reported with every subject and fingerprint. never    learn nothing; the host stays untrusted until --mcp-trust-ca. --mcp-trust-pin targets\|never. |
| `pin_verify_codes` | `[2, 19, 20]` | OpenSSL verify codes that mean "the issuer is unknown here": 2 unable to get issuer certificate, 19 self-signed certificate in chain, 20 unable to get local issuer certificate.  A wrong hostname (62) or an expired certificate (10) is never learned, whatever this says. |
| `store_dir` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_TRUST_DIR:-${cfg:paths.state_dir}/trust}"` | Where learned chains and the combined bundle are kept.  Delete anchor_subdir to forget every chain learned. |
| `anchor_subdir` | `"anchors"` |  |
| `bundle_filename` | `"ca-bundle.pem"` | Everything trusted, in one file: the host bundle, extra_ca and the learned chains.  Entries for a host that needed more than the host bundle name this file instead; every other entry is written as before. |
| `probe_timeout_seconds` | `8` |  |
| `chain_command` | `["openssl", "s_client", "-showcerts", "-connect", "{host}:{port}",…` | Reads the chain a server presents where Python cannot (before 3.13). {host} and {port} are substituted; skipped when the program is not installed. |
| `check_named_bundles` | `true` | Check every trust-store file an entry names -- this program's own, or one it brought with it (a reused registration, an agent's proposal, --mcp-trust-ca) -- against each https host the entry reaches, the way the strictest runtime reads it: partial chains off, so the chain must end at a self-signed root in the file.  partial_chain above is how *this program* verifies; this is how a server it registers will.  Python 3.13 and curl accept a chain that stops at any trusted certificate; Node does not.  smelt.example.net's NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS named a bundle holding "Example CA 2023.1" and "Example CA Root" but not the "Example Trust Root" above them: the server started, listed its tools, and failed every request with "fetch failed".  A file that falls short is replaced by the host bundle or this run's combined bundle, whichever carries the chain; both hold the host's store, where such a root usually lives. |
| `root_required_variables` | `["NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS"]` | Variables whose runtime accepts only a chain that ends at a self-signed root. When no bundle on this machine carries the chain for one of these, the entry cannot work at all, and refuse_incomplete_chain decides what happens.  Any other variable is only noted, since its runtime may accept the shorter chain. |
| `refuse_incomplete_chain` | `true` | Refuse such an entry -- in the stage, so the target keeps looking, and at publish.  false writes it anyway, with the reason in its notes. |
| `trial_names_host_bundle` | `true` | A trial names the bundle its entry will: the run's own where a host needed it, else this host's (as trust.env_for writes it) -- never nothing.  Node keeps its own store and ignores the host's, so an entry trialled bare failed with "fetch failed" though the entry it became named the host bundle. |

### `[mcp.trust.consumer]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | Trust follows the runtime that opens the connection (mcp_auto_discovery/consumer_trust.py).  A URL entry is opened by Claude Code itself, on Node: it trusts its own roots, the system store and NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS -- never this program's bundle.  openqa-example-net was verified here with a store holding the internal "Example Trust Root" and showed "Failed to connect -- UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY" in Claude Code on a machine without it.  For every https URL entry Claude Code cannot verify on its own, a bundle (what it is already given, plus each chain up to its root) is written beside .mcp.json and brought to every place a new terminal's Claude Code reads ([machine_env]); the log says each place and its outcome. |
| `variable` | `"NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS"` |  |
| `proactive` | `true` | Before Claude Code's own check (proactive), and again when that check fails with a trust failure ([mcp.registration.claude_check.failure_classes]). |
| `store_command` | `[]` | What Claude Code trusts on its own: its runtime's roots, asked of the runtime (if that cannot be asked: the public roots this program carries), and the system store (changing SSL_CERT_FILE changes Claude Code's verdict). Empty: the command [mcp.trust.runtime_stores] gives for `variable`. |
| `reads_system_store` | `true` |  |
| `bundle_dir` | `"trust"` |  |
| `bundle_filename` | `"claude-code-ca.pem"` |  |
| `repair_broken` | `true` | Every CA variable a new terminal or Claude Code's settings set to a file that cannot work (missing, or holding no certificate) is corrected: ~/.profile and /etc/profile.d exported SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE and NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS naming deleted /tmp bundles.  A store-replacing one goes back to the system's own bundle.  None is added that nobody set. |
| `trust_variables` | `["NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS", "SSL_CERT_FILE", "REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE", "CUR…` |  |
| `replacing_variables` | `["SSL_CERT_FILE", "REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE", "CURL_CA_BUNDLE"]` |  |
