### `[mcp.registration]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `path_root_never` | `["/", "~"]` | A path root that would stand for far more than one program's files is never used: "/" and the home folder (and any folder above it). |
| `repoint_by_relative_path` | `true` | A path an entry names that is not there is re-pointed by its own tail under this program's folders (the folder of .mcp.json, the servers' home, its own checkout) -- longest tail first, a folder and a file at least -- whatever the old folder was called (claude_ai_initialization, claude-ai-initialization, anything): an existing .mcp.json keeps working after a rename or move. |
| `own_reference_names` | `true` | Every ${NAME} an entry reads is a name only this program, or the user for that entry, sets.  bugzilla-example-com read ${BUGZILLA_API_KEY:-}: a shell exported a revoked BUGZILLA_API_KEY and it won over the key given for the entry; its ${SSL_CERT_FILE:-/etc/ssl/ca-bundle.pem} lost to a login shell's deleted /tmp bundle.  The key the server reads is kept; the variable it expands becomes owned_reference_template ({SLUG} = the entry's name), a trust bundle that is this machine's own reads trust_reference (set per machine by phase 1), and a session variable (SSH_AUTH_SOCK) or a name with path_variable_prefix or one of owned_prefixes is kept.  A credential Claude Code's settings hold under the old name is kept under the new one (carry_settings_value); one only a shell exports is not.  false writes the names the servers document. |
| `owned_reference_template` | `"{SLUG}_{NAME}"` |  |
| `trust_reference` | `"ICA_MCP_CA_BUNDLE"` |  |
| `resolve_unfound_commands` | `true` | A trust variable (SSL_CERT_FILE, REQUESTS_CA_BUNDLE, ...) holding the system bundle or one in this run's trust store is written ${<trust_reference>:-path} too -- never through the state directory's variable: gitlab.example.net's entry read ${ICA_STATE_DIR:-...}/trust/ca-bundle.pem, a file only the run machine had, and died at once anywhere else. A command written by a bare name the client's PATH does not find, but that this run resolved and launched (through paths.extra_bin_dirs), is written as the path that ran -- then named like any absolute path (${ICA_MCP_UVX:-...}). gitlab.example.net's entry said "uvx" while its trial ran /root/.local/bin/uvx, and the entry as written failed with "No such file or directory".  A name the client finds stays bare (the launcher form). |
| `owned_prefixes` | `[]` |  |
| `carry_settings_value` | `true` |  |
| `operator_reference_settings` | `["mcp.discovery.auth.bearer_token_ref"]` | Settings in which the operator names a credential variable on purpose ("env:NAME"): that name is theirs and is kept. |
| `own_references_in_file` | `true` | The final check makes every entry of the file what this run would write -- also the ones no write path touched (kept, hand-edited, older versions), which travel all the same: references renamed as above (own_references_in_file); a literal credential moved to Claude Code's settings env under the entry's own name, never over another value (move_literal_credentials_in_file); a stdio entry with no way to send a login given the slot its server reads one from -- its source, else the same package's other entries -- written optional (slot_missing_logins_in_file).  gitlab-example-net and bugzilla-opensuse-org were in the file with no credential slot at all. |
| `move_literal_credentials_in_file` | `true` |  |
| `slot_missing_logins_in_file` | `true` |  |
| `report_value_origins` | `true` | The final check logs, per entry, where each value it reads comes from on this machine: Claude Code's settings, a startup file's line, the entry's default, or unset -- names and places, never a value. |
| `scope_from_get` | `true` | Every `claude mcp remove` names the exact CLI scope -- from Claude Code's configuration, else the scope `claude mcp get` reports (scope_from_get, read with cli_scope_words) -- and none is run when no CLI scope holds the name: without a scope the CLI takes a project entry out of .mcp.json, and build-opensuse-org's own entry was removed that way as "a CLI copy". |
| `move_literal_secrets` | `true` | A written entry owns its files.  Bridges, manifests and CA bundles a server launches or reads from this run's scratch area (paths.work_dir) are moved to artifacts_home/<server>/ -- with the folder they sit in when it is the server's own -- and the entry names them there.  smelt.example.net's CA bundle and build.example.net's bridge lived in work/ only while cleanup spared them, and pointed nowhere once the project moved.  artifacts_home must lie outside the work directory; cleanup never touches it. A credential the project file holds as plain text (or as the default of ${NAME:-…}) -- pasted in by hand, or kept from an older entry -- is moved into Claude Code's settings.json env (0600) under the variable the entry reads, and the entry reads ${NAME}.  Never over a different value already there. |
| `adopt_existing_files` | `true` | An existing entry whose files are still in the scratch area has them moved to its own folder as soon as it is found, while they are there. |
| `replace_lost_files_cli_copies` | `true` | A claude CLI copy that launches a file which is gone is replaced by the written entry whose files are there: the CLI's copy is what Claude Code loads. |
| `never_empty_when_verified` | `true` | An address is never left with nothing while a server answered and was verified for it: one that settled nothing (it could not be asked what the address is for, or its access was never proved) is written when nothing else would be, and the verdict names it under NOT PROVED. |
| `skip_values_claude_has` | `true` | The verdict's "export …" and "named but unset" lists leave out every name a new terminal's Claude Code already has (its settings.json env, this program's env file): build-example-net was told to export a user name already kept there. |
| `verdict_reads_file` | `true` | Every view (address verdicts, the summary, "Not in .mcp.json") counts what the file holds for an address -- read back after publishing -- not only what this run registered: build-example-net was kept, working and in the file, and was reported missing from it. |
| `align_slots_in_file` | `true` | The final file check compares every entry's credential slots with what the script it launches reads -- written, kept or hand-edited: a slot never read, beside one credential variable it does read, is renamed to it; any other is reported ("never reaches the server").  A claude CLI copy so affected is replaced by the file's. |
| `carry_supplied_credentials` | `true` | A login the operator supplied is never dropped.  bugzilla-example-com's new entry worked as anybody (public bugs only) and the claude CLI copy carrying the API key was replaced by it.  A credential key an existing entry for the address carries -- that the new server reads (its source names it) or that the same launch carried -- is written optional (${NAME:-}), its value kept in Claude Code's settings env, never in the file; a CLI copy is replaced only once the file's entry carries the slot too. |
| `check_as_run` | `true` | The final file check reads every entry as a new terminal's Claude Code will run it on this machine: a ${ that is no ${NAME} or ${NAME:-default} (passed as literal text) is reported; a launched file, or a file an env value names, that is not there once expanded is pointed at the one file of that name in this program's own folders (the servers' home, bridges/), else reported with the variable that relocates it.  gitlab-example-net named a bridge three folders deep that no longer existed, and was judged broken. |
| `report_what_travels` | `true` | Say, at the end, what a copied .mcp.json needs beside it (the folders and files its entries name in its own folder: mcp-servers/, bridges/, a trust bundle) and which named paths each machine supplies itself, with the variable that relocates each.  The operator copies the file between machines. |
| `best_copy_speaks_for_name` | `true` | Two existing copies may share a name -- gitlab-example-net was a logged-in server in the claude CLI and an anonymous one in the project file.  The best proven (verified, usage score, proof) speaks for the name, and when it keeps its place it is the one written to the file, replacing the less proven copy. |
| `keeping_needs_proof` | `true` | A place is kept by proof, never by status: an existing entry that proved nothing this run (no login accepted, no task done) keeps it only while no candidate ranks above it on what is known ([mcp.discovery.auth.evidence]). Being registered, answering, or "connected" in Claude Code is no evidence -- build-opensuse-org's proxy, written by an earlier version, kept its place over the bridge that logs in the way the address asks. |
| `connected_holds_place` | `false` | Claude Code reporting an existing entry "connected" holds no place: a status, not proof.  gitlab.example.net's bridge was refused for an old claude CLI copy that connected before the run -- one this run had discarded (it named a file not on the machine) -- and .mcp.json ended with no gitlab entry.  true brings the old rule back. |
| `unjudged_is_keepable` | `false` | Kept means written: an existing entry may keep its place only when a copy of it was judged this run and can be recorded in .mcp.json.  One this run never judged (or discarded) holds nothing -- gitlab.example.net's discarded CLI copy kept its place and could not be written, and the address ended with no entry. |
| `failed_copy_holds_nothing` | `true` | A copy tried this run that neither works nor waits for its credential holds no place, and the copy that keeps it replaces it in .mcp.json: confluence-example-com's file copy (a URL answering a login page) spoke for the name over its working CLI copy and stayed in the file. |
| `one_keep_gate` | `true` | One gate every keep rule passes: an existing copy may hold its place only when nothing proved it unusable, it is a different server from the candidate (any copy of the name), and it can be written to .mcp.json.  build-opensuse-org's fresh client bridge was refused for an unusable copy of itself. |
| `compare_after_carrying` | `true` | Values an existing entry supplies (a default user name) count for the candidate too when the two are compared -- they are carried into what is written. |
| `never_an_empty_address` | `true` | Never an empty address: when the final file check finds an address with a server but no entry, the best candidate this run refused that works or waits for its credential is written (and said).  Two rounds ended "has a server but ./.mcp.json has no entry" and only reported it. |
| `credential_files_may_be_absent` | `true` | A path a credential slot names (an SSH key, a client certificate) may be absent on the machine that runs the program: it is the operator's credential, supplied per machine like a token -- never "a file that is not there". build-example-net's SSH-signing bridge was refused for /root/.ssh/id_ed25519 and a password bridge the API host does not accept was written instead. credential_file_slots: env keys naming a credential file, beside every secret name. |
| `credential_file_slots` | `['(^\|_)SSH_KEY($\|_)', '(^\|_)KEY_?FILE$', '(^\|_)(CLIENT_)?CERT(IFICA…` |  |
| `say_unoffered_login` | `true` | Never ask the operator for a value that cannot work: an entry whose slots send a kind of login the address offers nowhere is reported as such, not as "export X".  build-opensuse-org's report asked for EXTRA_HEADERS, and a Bearer token went there for an API that takes Basic. |
| `repoint_before_trial` | `true` | A file an existing entry launches or names that is not there is found again (the one file of that name in this program's folders) before the entry is trialled -- not only in the final file check.  sd-example-com's working bridge was called broken for a path one folder too deep. |
| `entry_files_beside_file` | `true` | Every file an entry names in this program's state or scratch area -- the run's trust bundle, the configuration folder a repair gave a server -- is copied into the servers' home beside .mcp.json before the entry is written, and named portably.  A copied .mcp.json named the state folder's bundle and a scratch-area config folder, which exist on no other machine. |
| `entry_files_max_bytes` | `50000000` | Programs (the venv, launchers -- phase 1's on every machine) are never copied; a file or folder heavier than this stays where it is. |
| `own_files` | `true` |  |
| `artifacts_home` | `"mcp-servers"` | Relative means beside the file the entries are written to (mcp.mcp_json_path): the files travel with the file.  Copying .mcp.json to another machine left gitlab-example-net's bridge behind in the state folder; it was pointed by hand at an older script that read another variable, and its token never reached GitLab.  ICA_MCP_SERVERS names the folder; phase 1 gives it this machine's path (install.machine_paths).  Must lie outside the work directory. |
| `legacy_artifacts_homes` | `["${cfg:paths.state_dir}/mcp-servers"]` | Homes an earlier version kept entries' files in: files found there are moved into artifacts_home too, so an older entry travels with the file as well. |
| `keep_credentials_in` | `"settings"` | Other words for a transport -- an agent's, a registry's -- and the one this program registers for each.  The entry's type is the transport its handshake was proved over; else the candidate's word through this table; a word that is unknown or contradicts the entry (stdio beside a url) never decides: a url entry is HTTP, a command entry stdio.  openqa.example.net's and developers.google.com's endpoints were written "type": "stdio" with a url, and Claude Code dropped both. Every entry is checked the way Claude Code reads it before it is written or registered: an entry Claude Code would skip at load is refused -- never written, never registered, the one already in place left as it was.  First the shape each type must and may have (entry_shapes), then Claude Code's own validation: the entry is added to a throw-away configuration directory (config_dir_variable) with add_command, so nothing real changes and the judge is the program that will load the file. A credential an existing entry carried as a literal (or a ${NAME:-default}) is never written to .mcp.json, which holds references only; it is kept where Claude Code reads it -- "settings": its own settings.json env (mode 0600), under the variable the entry reads -- unless the shell exports that variable, settings hold another value for it, or this run saw it refused.  "none" keeps nothing.  sd-example-com, openqa-example-net and gitlab-example-net had come out "waiting for a credential" although the operator had supplied one. |
| `keep_supplied_values` | `true` | ...and so is every other value an existing entry for the address supplied that the new entry reads as ${NAME} with no value of its own and a new terminal would not have (mcp.registration.fresh_env): a user name, a setting. build-example-net's user name was dropped with the entry it replaced, and only the run's shell still had it. |
| `reshape_entries` | `true` | After the last write, an entry Claude Code would skip only for its shape -- "type": "stdio" beside a url -- is given the shape its own fields say (and a key that type does not take is dropped), whichever run wrote it. |
| `validate_entries` | `true` |  |
| `restore_on_failure` | `true` | A CLI copy removed to make way for a new entry is put back when the new one cannot be added: an address is never left with nothing because a replacement failed (openqa-example-net's was removed, the add was refused, and the run said "registered"). |
| `connected_is_not_working` | `true` | An existing entry Claude Code connects to holds no place by itself: when neither it nor its replacement proved anything, the replacement built for the API the host was seen to serve takes the name. |
| `held_must_be_recordable` | `true` | The choice to keep an existing entry in place of a refused replacement is the condition for writing it: it is recorded in .mcp.json too, in its portable form, whatever it proved.  An existing entry that cannot be recorded portably holds no place.  And the end-of-run file check repairs: an address with a server and no entry gets its answered existing entry written.  github-com was kept because it answered, never written because it was neither verified nor connected, and the check only reported the gap. |
| `repair_missing_entries` | `true` |  |
| `repair_from_untried_existing` | `true` | ...and when nothing this run tried answered, a registration for the address that this run never tried (gitlab-example-net's bridge, one tier below a server the re-check withdrew) is tried as written, and recorded if it answers. |
| `validate_with_claude` | `true` |  |
| `config_dir_variable` | `"CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR"` |  |
| `entry_shapes` | `{ stdio = { required = ["command"], allowed = ["type", "command", "…` |  |
| `transport_aliases` | `{ http = "streamable-http", https = "streamable-http", streamable-h…` |  |
| `fold_copies` | `true` | One server, one entry, in every mode: copies of one server -- the same package (read with mcp.env_contract.package_sources' launchers, versions aside) reaching the same hosts, or the same URL on the same transport, launched with other flags -- are folded into the best-proved of them; the copies stay start-up fallbacks.  bugzilla.example.com got two entries for one `uvx mcp-bugzilla`, one with --read-only added.  Different servers are never folded: how many an address keeps is still --exhaustive-mcp/--the-best-mcp's. |
| `prefer_installed_program` | `true` | An entry whose launch command is a build in the agent workspace runs the program of the same name on the PATH instead, when that one answers alike: build-opensuse-org ran a scratch build of osc-mcp beside /usr/local/bin/osc-mcp. |
| `name_by_role` | `true` | A generic login slot is named for what it holds -- {SLUG}_USERNAME and {SLUG}_PASSWORD (mcp.bridge.generated.auth.variable_template), the names the client bridge for the same service reads -- when no other slot of the entry holds the same, and is described as that account's user name or password: osc-mcp's OSC_MCP_PASSWORD was asked for as BUILD_OPENSUSE_ORG_OSC_MCP_PASSWORD with "shape unknown".  A vendor's own name is kept, and a token or key keeps the name its server gives it: its kind is not known from a name. |
| `complete_slots` | `true` | Every entry, before it is written, is checked against what it launches reads (a generated bridge's manifest); a missing credential slot is added as ${NAME:-} and named as needed -- an entry is never written short. |
| `verify_written` | `true` | Once everything is written, every entry of this run's addresses is read back from the file and checked against what it launches reads; a missing slot is added in place.  A check on one write path is not a check on the result: build-example-net reached the file without its username by a path the publish check did not guard. |
| `say_how_to_move` | `true` | Each server's summary says which variable moves each machine-specific path its entry names (${VAR:-/path} in command, args or env) -- printed, not only kept in the report. |
| `replace_divergent_cli_copies` | `true` | ...and the claude CLI's copy of such an entry -- which loads before the file's -- is replaced by the file's entry when it lacks a slot, or differs from the entry this run wrote and proved.  Each replacement is reported. |
| `keep_server_slot_keys` | `true` | A local server's credential slot keeps the key the server reads; only the variable it points at is named for the operator (osc-mcp's slot was renamed BUILD_OPENSUSE_ORG_OSC_MCP_USER, a variable osc-mcp never reads). |
| `read_trial_source` | `true` | ...and the variable it points at is the one the trial read, when the slot was declared as another variable that holds a value (env:GITLAB_EXAMPLE_NET_TOKEN for GITLAB_PERSONAL_ACCESS_TOKEN): the trial's login was accepted from it, and an entry reading a name nothing sets starts the server without a token. |
| `describe_from_manifest` | `true` | A credential slot of a generated bridge is described from the bridge's own manifest (its auth scheme and variables), so a kept entry is described as the generated one was: sd-example-com's token fell back to "shape unknown". |
| `retrial_rewritten` | `true` | An existing entry that failed is trialled again before anything is written when this run has since rewritten a file it names (a regenerated manifest or bridge script): a verdict taken before the file changed is not a verdict. |
| `current_keeps_name` | `true` | Several servers written for one address: what is registered now keeps its own name, and the others take the suffixes -- the operator's tool names do not move. |
| `same_address_one_instance` | `true` | Entries written for the same address in one run are one instance: they share its credential variables rather than one being renamed per entry. |
| `name_by_role_parts` | `["USERNAME", "PASSWORD"]` |  |
| `fold_script_extensions` | `[".py", ".js", ".mjs", ".cjs", ".ts", ".rb", ".sh"]` | A script an interpreter runs (one of these extensions) is one server by its file name and the hosts it reaches, wherever the file lives: one client bridge for build.opensuse.org was written twice, from two directories. |
| `require_paths_exist` | `true` | Refuse to register an entry naming a path that is not there when it is written.  Verification proves a command worked *at that instant*; this is the separate question of whether it still does.  It also catches the case that motivated it -- a virtualenv built to trial a package, registered by absolute path, and gone by the time anything tried to start it. |
| `verify_as_written` | `true` | Launch each finished entry, exactly as written, and record whether it starts. The last gate, and the only one that tests the artefact rather than the thing it was derived from.  A candidate is trialled with the environment discovery assembled; the entry is what ships, with ${VAR} placeholders that may resolve to nothing.  Three servers passed every earlier check and then died on start-up, each written with one variable the proven launch had not carried -- so nothing that ran had ever run what shipped. This check reports; whether a failure withholds the entry is require_entry_starts, below.  The same check runs inside each stage first (mcp.healing), for working candidates and for local ones waiting for a credential alike, so one that cannot start never settles its target. |
| `require_entry_starts` | `true` | Refuse an entry that still will not start after every repair.  Only an entry proven to start is written: one that cannot is not a configuration, it is a line that will fail in front of the operator with "Connection closed" and no reason.  Asked in the stage, where the refusal reopens the lower tiers so the target keeps looking, and again at publish, where start_fallbacks below hands its place to the next candidate this run proved. false restores the older behaviour, in both places, of keeping it, writing it anyway and reporting the failure -- which is what shipped two dead openQA entries. |
| `start_fallbacks` | `2` | When an entry is refused at publish because it does not start, how many of the other candidates this run proved for the address (working ones first, then ones waiting for a credential, in tier order) to try in its place.  One failure must not leave an address with nothing while another proven server is in hand: confluence.example.com ended empty that way.  0 tries none. |
| `keep_answering_existing` | `true` | An existing entry that answered during this run keeps its place against a candidate this run did not prove -- one only waiting for a credential, whose login was never accepted.  smelt.example.net's working mcp-graphql entry was overwritten by a bridge waiting for a token, built for an API smelt does not serve.  The held-back candidate is reported with how to prove it.  An entry this run proved unusable (it does not start, its account has no API access) is replaced as before; so is one of the same launch.  false lets an unproven candidate replace it. |
| `compare_credential_values` | `true` | Compare the credential *values* entries send (by fingerprint only, the parts of a Basic credential included), not only the variable names: the same login sent to two different services is reported.  build-example-net sent build.opensuse.org's user and password, as base64 under a name of its own. |
| `optional_unset_settings` | `true` | A setting's ${NAME} that nothing sets is written ${NAME:-} (empty when unset), or left out when the server was proven to start without it.  Claude Code passes an unset ${NAME} as literal text, and BUGZILLA_AUTH_MODE reached the server as '${BUGZILLA_AUTH_MODE}'.  Credentials keep their ${NAME} slots. |
| `recheck_command` | `"initialize-claude-ai run --phases 4 --mcp-recheck {host}"` | How the checklist of the operator's own steps says to prove a step done ({host} filled): a recheck tries only what is there, in seconds. |
| `check_through_claude` | `true` | The last check, after an entry is written: a short non-interactive Claude Code session (claude -p) is given exactly that entry and asked to call one usage task's tool, and the tool's own answer -- read from the session's events, never the model's summary -- is judged like a usage task.  Claude Code launches a server differently from this program (${NAME} expands only from the environment it started with, its own working directory and trust stores), and several failures showed only there.  Variables the entry reads are looked for first, with no model request: a missing one is reported with "export it in the shell you start Claude Code from, then restart Claude Code".  A check that cannot run (no claude, not logged in, out of quota, a timeout) is inconclusive and never fails an entry.  It costs one small request per entry. |
| `replace_unproved_existing` | `true` | An existing entry whose access never proved anything -- every call empty or unchecked -- is replaced, in the file *and* in the claude CLI, when a bridge for the target's other API proved access and took its place.  sd.example.com's mcp-atlassian answered [] to everything with a working token and a dead one alike; where it lives in the CLI, the CLI copy would otherwise go on loading in place of the bridge, because the CLI takes precedence over the file. |
| `name_undeclared_credentials` | `true` | A credential-like variable a candidate's script reads but does not declare is named to the operator as needed -- with the others it waits for -- unless the candidate is proved to work without it or the variable is already exported. sd.example.com's agent-written bridge read SD_EXAMPLE_COM_USERNAME and SD_EXAMPLE_COM_PASSWORD, declared neither, and was registered as if it needed only a token. |
| `require_address_in_entry` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_REQUIRE_ADDRESS:-true}"` | Refuse an entry that carries no address, or whose address is not the target's. The question an operator asks of any entry is "is this pointed at my server", and `npx -y @kubb/mcp` -- registered as the MCP server for confluence.example.com -- could not answer it: a real MCP server, for something else entirely, with nothing in the entry that could ever reach Confluence. A URL may be on a *different* host, provided that host answered as an MCP endpoint when probed: github.com is served from api.githubcopilot.com and developers.google.com from developerknowledge.googleapis.com, and an earlier version of this check refused both.  A launcher may not -- it is never probed at an address, so unlike a URL nothing about running it shows where it points, and a package whose name merely suits the target is not evidence. See mcp_auto_discovery/grounding.py. |
| `allow_bare_origin` | `false` | Whether a bare origin -- https://host with no path -- may be registered as an HTTP endpoint without having completed a handshake.  It may not: MCP endpoints live at a path, and a site's front door answering 401 to an anonymous POST is a login page, not a discovery.  https://confluence.example.com was registered exactly that way and no credential could ever have made it work.  A URL that actually handshaked at the origin is unaffected. |
| `tls_weakening_env` | `[ …` | Environment variables that switch certificate verification off.  These are never written into an entry: .mcp.json is copied between machines, and a file that silently disables TLS wherever it lands is not something to hand someone. NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED reached a real entry as "${NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED}" -- an unset placeholder, so it did nothing until the day somebody exported that name for an unrelated reason, and then it would have turned off verification for the whole Node process.  A server that genuinely needs a private CA is a trust-store problem to report, not a flag to carry: see mcp.bridge.generated.ca_bundle for the supported way. |
| `tls_weakening_patterns` | `["NO_VERIFY", "SKIP_VERIFY", "REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED", "INSECURE"]` | ...and the shapes of the ones nobody has met yet, matched as substrings of the variable's name.  An exact list always lags: REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED reached a real entry as "false" because the list knew only NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED. |
| `durable_venv_roots` | `[ …` | Directories under which a virtualenv is kept on purpose, so an entry naming a path inside one is host-bound (registered, reported as not portable) rather than refused as a trial venv.  Everything else holding pyvenv.cfg is still taken to be scratch, and the trial sandbox always is, whatever is listed here. openqa.example.net was lost to this: phase 1 installs into its own venv where the system Python is externally managed, the program runs from it, the bridge it generated named that interpreter -- and the entry was refused as "built to trial a package".  Unset (empty) entries are ignored.  The venv this program is running from is added too; see trust_running_venv. |
| `trust_running_venv` | `true` | Treat the virtualenv this program runs from as durable: if it went away, so would the program, and its interpreter is what a generated bridge is proved with (mcp.bridge.generated.interpreter, when empty). |
| `interpreter_variable` | `"ICA_MCP_PYTHON"` | The variable used for the interpreter a generated bridge is launched with. It is a system binary, so unlike the roots above it is matched whole rather than as a prefix -- and unlike /etc/ssl/ca-bundle.pem it is a choice this program made: pinned absolute because a bare `python3` resolved to a different interpreter, with a different certificate store, on the machine that later launched the bridge.  Written as ${VARIABLE:-<that interpreter>}, which keeps the pin and lets another machine say where its own lives. Empty leaves the interpreter as a plain absolute path. |
| `launcher_variable_template` | `"ICA_MCP_{LAUNCHER}"` | ...and the same treatment for a launcher binary -- uvx, npx, node, docker. `{LAUNCHER}` is the binary's own name, upper-cased, so `uvx` resolved at /home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin/uvx is written "${ICA_MCP_UVX:-/home/linuxbrew/.linuxbrew/bin/uvx}". This was the very first failure reported against this program and it was still in the file: an entry naming /root/.local/bin/uvx, correct on the machine that wrote it, `ENOENT` on the next one -- which Claude Code shows as `failed - Connection closed`, saying nothing about a missing binary. The interpreter already had this treatment; the launcher, which appears far more often, did not. Whole path rather than the containing directory, matching the interpreter: one variable means one binary. A launcher this host does not have is not named at all, and a bare `uvx` found through PATH is already portable. Empty turns the rewriting off. |
| `name_every_absolute_path` | `true` | ...and finally the general rule the three settings above are special cases of: EVERY absolute path in an entry is a fact about one machine, so every one of them is written "${VARIABLE:-<the path here>}". It took four reports to get here, each a path nobody had thought to cover: the bridge bundle (a root), /usr/bin/python3 (the interpreter), /root/.local/bin/uvx (a launcher), and OPENQA_VERIFY=/home/.../chain.pem -- a PEM belonging to a third-party package, under no root and matching no binary.  Enumerating kinds of path is a losing game; the next entry holds a kind nobody enumerated. The variable is named after, in order: the configured root it sits under, the binary it is, the environment variable holding it, or its own basename.  The default keeps the entry identical in effect where it was written -- an unset ${VAR:-default} yields exactly the original string -- which is also why this is safe to apply broadly. false restores the older behaviour of touching only paths under a root above. |
| `path_variable_prefix` | `"ICA_MCP"` | Prefix for a variable named from a basename, when nothing better applies. |
| `path_variables_file` | `"mcp-path-variables.json"` | Every name derived from a file's own name (/usr/bin/python3.13 -> ICA_MCP_PYTHON3_13) is remembered here, under the state directory, so an entry read back without its default still resolves; a derived name not on record is spelled back (_ as ., - or itself) and looked up on PATH. |
| `add_command` | `["{claude}", "mcp", "add-json", "{name}", "{json}"]` | `mcp add-json` takes stdio, http and sse in one uniform shape, which is why it is preferred over `mcp add`. Flags verified against `claude mcp add --help`. |
| `scope_flag` | `["--scope", "{scope}"]` |  |
| `list_command` | `["{claude}", "mcp", "list"]` |  |
| `get_command` | `["{claude}", "mcp", "get", "{name}"]` | Asked about every registered server at the end of the phase: it makes Claude Code connect the way it will next session and print what it found, which is the one verification this program does not perform with its own client. |
| `remove_command` | `["{claude}", "mcp", "remove", "{name}"]` | Used to take back an entry *this run's own add_command* registered and then withdrew (see refuse_shared_claims below; scope_flag is appended), and to retire an existing registration that this run proved is not its address's (see retire_refused_existing below; no scope flag, the CLI finds the name). |
| `connected_markers` | `["connected"]` | How that output is read.  Matched case-insensitively; failures are looked for first, so "failed to connect" is never mistaken for "connected". |
| `failed_markers` | `["failed to connect", "connection failed", "not connected", "needs…` | A status Claude Code marks with a warning is not a working server: "! Connected · tools fetch failed — Request timed out" means its tools could not even be listed.  build-opensuse-org's proxy was read as connected that way and kept its place over a bridge that works. |
| `degraded_patterns` | `['(^\|[\s\-:])!\s*connected']` |  |
| `timeout_seconds` | `90` |  |
| `overwrite_existing` | `false` | Re-register a server that is already known under the same name. |
| `replace_literal_cli_copies` | `true` | A claude CLI copy of a name this run wrote that holds a credential as a literal (a token pasted into `claude mcp add`) loads in place of the file's entry and travels with copied configuration: it is removed, from every scope, when the written entry was proved and every credential it reads is exported. |
| `keep_more_proven_existing` | `true` | An existing entry shown short of its job (a usage task failed) still stays over a replacement that passed less of the contract and proved no login -- build-example-net's openapi-proxy still searched packages, and was replaced by a server that could do nothing until a variable nobody exports was set. |
| `record_kept_entries` | `true` | A kept CLI entry that verified, or that Claude Code reports connected, is written into the project file too (portably: credentials as ${VAR}) when the file has no entry of that name -- every working server ends up in both places. developers-google-com stayed in the CLI only and vanished from .mcp.json. |
| `rejudge_identity` | `true` | A proven server refused only because nothing yet tied it to the address is kept aside and judged again as the run finds evidence (a documented or linked endpoint, an admitted copy of the same server). |
| `inherit_credential_slots` | `true` | The kept copy of one server carries the credential slots (references, never values) of a copy that has them, when it has none of its own. |
| `check_in_file` | `true` | After each address, and again at the end of the run: every address that has a server has an entry in .mcp.json -- an entry written but lost is written again, a kept working one is recorded, and an address left without one is reported with every refusal.  bugzilla-opensuse-org, developers-google-com and confluence-example-com each went missing a different way. |
| `refuse_shared_claims` | `true` | One endpoint claimed for several unrelated addresses is none of theirs. https://api.mcp.ai/p_examplep_administradores -- a third party's tool that names no Example host -- was registered for six Example hosts and github.com in one run, and all this program said was "duplicate".  When the same entry turns up for addresses of different organisations (different registrable domains) and its verdict rests only on a claim -- one of shared_claim_bases -- the later ones are refused and the entries already published for the earlier ones are withdrawn: out of .mcp.json (restoring what the file held before) and out of the CLI via remove_command.  An entry that names its address, or whose server names it, is never affected, whoever else uses the same package. |
| `shared_claim_bases` | `["vendor", "unprobed"]` | Which grounding verdicts are "only a claim" (see grounding.BASIS_*): "vendor" is provenance -- documentation or a registry entry said so -- and "unprobed" is a verdict still waiting on a probe.  The others ("host", "named", "server", "found-serving", "organisation") are evidence about one address. |
| `shared_secret_template` | `"{SLUG}_{NAME}"` | A credential belongs to one instance.  jira.example.com and sd.example.com run the same package, which reads JIRA_PERSONAL_TOKEN; written through for both, one exported value had to be two instances' tokens, so at most one could work -- and the operator pasted a literal token into each entry instead.  When an entry already in the file (or written earlier in this run) reads a credential variable for a *different* host, this entry keeps the key the server reads and points it at this template instead.  {SLUG} is the entry's name in variable form, {NAME} the variable it would otherwise read. |
| `retire_refused_existing` | `true` | A registration already on this machine that this run proved is *not* its address's is retired, so no later session keeps loading it.  "Proved" is narrow on purpose: it answered as an MCP server, it connects only to hosts that belong neither to the address nor to its organisation, and the registration gate refused it -- the shape of the six api.mcp.ai entries.  An entry that is merely down, or that names no address at all, is reported and left alone.  Only names this program gives the address (its FQDN name, with or without a suffix) are touched; any other name is the operator's, and is reported with the command to remove it.  The .mcp.json entry is removed only if unchanged since it was read; a CLI entry via remove_command.  With it off, every such entry is reported and none is removed. |

### `[mcp.registration.cli_scope_words]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `local` | `'(?i)\blocal\b'` |  |
| `user` | `'(?i)\buser\b'` |  |

### `[mcp.registration.identity]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `gateway_markers` | `["marketplace", "catalog", "catalogue"]` | Whole words in a server's tool names or instructions that make it a catalog of other servers' tools -- such a server "names" every product it can reach. |
| `accept_unanswered` | `true` | A server that has not given an answer to read (one behind a credential wall) keeps its claim for now; refuse_shared_claims still watches it.  False refuses every claimed third-party server that has not answered. |
| `organisation_needs_tie` | `true` | One organisation runs many services: a sibling host of the target's organisation is its server only with a tie -- the sibling carries only generic labels (api., mcp.; mcp.packages.generic_host_labels), the target is the organisation's own host, the sibling carries one of the target's product words, or the server's answer names one.  dashboard.qa.example.net (Example's QA dashboard) became smelt.example.net's "native endpoint" on "same organisation" alone and closed the tiers that held smelt's working GraphQL server.  false restores the organisation-alone rule. |
| `third_party_needs_host` | `true` | On a host that is neither the target's nor its organisation's, and with nobody speaking for the target (its own documentation, landing page, .well-known, llms.txt, or a registry entry in its own namespace -- not com.githubcard/*), the server's own answer must name the target's address itself (a resource URI, a default, its instructions): a product word is what a service *about* the product says too.  github.com was given githubcard.com's card maker ("turns a GitHub user or repository into a card") in place of GitHub's own server.  false accepts a product word as before. |
| `prefix_needs_listing` | `true` | A domain whose name merely begins with the organisation's word is the organisation's only when listed below: githubcard.com begins with "github" exactly as api.githubcopilot.com does, and com.googleapis.* is Google's while com.githubcard/* is not -- no rule over names tells them apart, so which domains an organisation owns is kept here as data.  A whole label (docs.github.com) always counts.  false reads every such prefix as the organisation's, as before. |
| `foreign_login_refuses` | `true` | A launcher believed only on its own words (or a third party's), whose every login variable names another organisation -- a word outside login_generic_words that is none of the target's words or labels -- logs in there, not to the target: github.com got an Apify scraper about GitHub organisations (APIFY_TOKEN).  An entry configured for the target itself, or a login naming nobody (API_ACCESS_TOKEN), is never refused by this. |
| `login_generic_words` | `["API", "KEY", "KEYS", "TOKEN", "TOKENS", "ACCESS", "PERSONAL", "SE…` |  |

### `[mcp.registration.identity.organisation_domains]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `github` | `["githubcopilot.com", "githubusercontent.com", "githubassets.com"]` |  |
| `google` | `["googleapis.com", "googleusercontent.com", "googlesource.com"]` |  |

### `[mcp.registration.path_variables]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `ICA_MCP_SERVERS` | `"${cfg:mcp.registration.artifacts_home}"` |  |
| `ICA_MCP_ARTIFACTS` | `"${cfg:mcp.agent.workspace}/artifacts"` |  |
| `ICA_MCP_WORKSPACE` | `"${cfg:mcp.agent.workspace}"` |  |
| `ICA_MCP_BRIDGES` | `"${cfg:mcp.bridge.output_dir}"` |  |
| `ICA_WORK_DIR` | `"${cfg:paths.work_dir}"` |  |
| `ICA_STATE_DIR` | `"${cfg:paths.state_dir}"` |  |
| `ICA_MCP_PROJECT` | `"."` | The folder holding .mcp.json itself -- where this program usually lives, its bridges/, trust/ and bin/ files included.  A path under it is written as ${ICA_MCP_PROJECT:-<absolute>}/..., so renaming, moving or cloning the folder (claude_ai_initialization, claude-ai-initialization, anything) breaks no entry: phase 1 (and phase 4) set the variable to where the folder is now whenever the written default is not there.  Never for "/" or the home folder (mcp.registration.path_root_never). |

### `[mcp.ranking]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `stability_probes` | `2` | Extra handshakes per URL candidate, to measure stability rather than assume it.  0 scores on the one handshake discovery already did.  Never applied to a stdio candidate: re-launching third-party code to collect a statistic is not a trade this tool makes on someone's machine. |
| `probe_timeout_seconds` | `8` |  |
| `latency_target_seconds` | `1.0` | A handshake at or under the target is as good as instant; at the ceiling it scores zero.  Seconds. |
| `latency_ceiling_seconds` | `8.0` |  |
| `stability_latency_share` | `0.3` | Within the stability aspect, how much is latency rather than success rate. |
| `functionality_target` | `12` | Tools + resources + prompts that count as a fully featured server; more than this does not keep adding to the score. |
| `capability_target` | `4` | Advertised initialize capabilities that count as complete coverage. |
| `functionality_capability_share` | `0.25` | Within the functionality aspect, how much is capabilities rather than count. |
| `stdio_transport_score` | `0.7` | Transport currency, and how much of the protocol aspect is the negotiated version rather than the transport. |
| `sse_transport_score` | `0.4` |  |
| `unknown_protocol_score` | `0.5` |  |
| `protocol_version_share` | `0.5` |  |

### `[mcp.ranking.weights]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `functionality` | `3.0` | Abundant functionality: tools, resources, prompts, capabilities. |
| `usability` | `2.0` | Easy to use: a URL is called, a local process is looked after. |
| `configuration` | `2.0` | Smooth configuration: installs, variables to export, custom headers. |
| `stability` | `3.0` | Stable connection: measured success rate and latency. |
| `security` | `3.0` | More secure: TLS, whose code runs, whose host it is. |
| `protocol` | `1.5` | Current transport and protocol version. |
| `provenance` | `1.5` | Who is behind it -- see origin_scores. |

### `[mcp.ranking.penalties]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `local_process` | `0.4` | usability: a server that is a process, not an address. |
| `unnamed` | `0.1` | usability: no server name, no instructions -- harder to know what it is for. |
| `no_instructions` | `0.1` |  |
| `install_step` | `0.2` | configuration: per command that must be run, variable exported, header set. |
| `secret_to_export` | `0.25` |  |
| `custom_header` | `0.1` |  |
| `encoded_credential` | `0.3` | configuration: per credential the operator must encode by hand -- a header list, a base64'd user:password (secret_policy.carrier_patterns).  A server that asks for the parts by name and builds the header itself outranks one that needs `Authorization:Basic <base64 of user:password>` typed into a variable; build.example.net's API_HEADERS held a bare token instead.  0 = off. |
| `password_when_token` | `0.2` | configuration: a candidate that needs a password, when the service issues a token that can read (mcp.discovery.products.*.logins) -- a token is scoped and revocable, and needs no password in the environment. |
| `host_bound` | `0.3` | configuration: the entry names an absolute path on this machine rather than a launcher that fetches what it needs.  .mcp.json exists to be copied, and a path does not travel -- `uvx <package>` works on any host, a venv under this program's state directory works on exactly one. |
| `cleartext` | `0.6` | security: cleartext to a public host puts every request, and any bearer token on it, on the wire in the open.  Loopback is exempt. |
| `insecure_tls` | `0.5` | security: the endpoint only answered once certificate verification was turned off.  It is a real endpoint and it is reported as one, but an unverifiable certificate is an unauthenticated peer -- fix the trust store, then re-run. |
| `executes_code` | `0.35` | security: a package that runs locally is a larger trust surface than a call. |
| `third_party_host` | `0.25` | security: an endpoint on someone else's host is not the host you asked about. |

### `[mcp.ranking.origin_scores]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `endpoint` | `1.0` |  |
| `package` | `0.75` |  |
| `bridge` | `0.45` |  |
| `strategy` | `0.3` |  |

### `[mcp.protocol]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `versions` | `["2026-07-28", "2025-11-25", "2025-06-18", "2025-03-26", "2024-11-05"]` | Offered newest-first; a server that rejects one is retried with the next. Source: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification |
| `client_name` | `"initialize-claude-ai-discovery"` |  |
| `client_version` | `""` | Empty: this program's own version (initialize_claude_ai.__version__). |
| `protocol_version_header` | `"MCP-Protocol-Version"` | Sent on every HTTP request after initialize, per the transports spec. |
| `session_header` | `"Mcp-Session-Id"` |  |
| `ping_method` | `"ping"` | Sent after the handshake when nothing else was asked, to prove the session carries traffic both ways. Empty disables it. |
| `accept_header` | `"application/json, text/event-stream"` | The spec requires BOTH media types on a POST to a Streamable HTTP endpoint. |
| `sse_accept_header` | `"text/event-stream"` |  |

### `[mcp.address]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `resolve` | `true` | Send one cheap request to each address and follow the redirects, so that "example.com" becomes whatever the server says it really is.  Turn this off in an air-gapped environment, or when the address is already exact. |
| `timeout_seconds` | `6` | Budget for that single request. Short: it is a courtesy, not the search. |
| `try_alternate_scheme` | `true` | When the address does not answer at all, try the other scheme.  http is only ever upgraded to https, never the other way round for a public host. |
| `local_suffixes` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_LOCAL_SUFFIXES:-}"` | DNS zones that are on your own network.  --mcp-server takes *any* address, and four decisions turn on whether the one you gave is local or public: whether a bearer token may travel over cleartext, whether cleartext costs the endpoint points in the ranking, whether the developer ports below are probed, and whether a bare name defaults to https.  Loopback, RFC 1918, link-local, .local, .internal, .lan and .home.arpa are recognised already; add your own here (comma separated in the variable) if your internal zone is .corp, .intra, or a registered domain served split-horizon.  Getting this wrong in the cautious direction is safe -- a public host treated as public -- so nothing is guessed from resolver configuration; it is yours to declare. |
| `loopback_hosts` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_LOOPBACK_HOSTS:-}"` | Extra names that mean this machine, beyond localhost and ::1. |
| `local_suffixes_replace` | `false` | true drops the built-in zones instead of adding to them, for the rare host where one of those conventions is somebody else's public domain. |

### `[mcp.grounding]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `multi_part_suffixes` | `[ …` | Public suffixes longer than one label (co.uk, com.au, co.jp ...). The registrable domain -- the organisation -- is one label more, so api.example.co.uk and www.example.co.uk are both example.co.uk, while example.co.uk and other.co.uk are two organisations, not one called "co.uk". It decides whether a sibling host's address is believed (with a flag) or refused.  Always in force; the public suffix list below is added to it. |
| `public_suffix_file` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_PUBLIC_SUFFIX_FILE:-/usr/share/publicsuffix…` | The full public suffix list (https://publicsuffix.org), read when this file exists -- openSUSE/Fedora: publicsuffix, Debian/Ubuntu: publicsuffix (/usr/share/publicsuffix/public_suffix_list.dat).  Missing or unreadable means only multi_part_suffixes above.  "" turns it off. |
| `public_suffix_sections` | `["icann"]` | Which sections of that list count.  "icann" holds the registries' own suffixes (co.uk, kawasaki.jp).  "private" adds hosting platforms that give each customer a subdomain (github.io, *.cloudfront.net): with it, two customers of one platform are two organisations -- stricter, and it moves the organisation of every address on such a platform to the customer's label. |

### `[mcp.secret_policy]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `path_is_never_a_secret` | `true` | A value that is one absolute path is where something lies (a key file, a bundle), never the secret itself, whatever its variable is called -- the one rule every guard asks.  build-example-net's ${..._OBS_SSH_KEY:-/root/.ssh/id_ed25519} was withheld from its trial and then moved out of the file as a "literal". |
| `sensitive_words` | `["key", "token", "secret", "password", "passwd", "credential", "aut…` | What counts as a credential -- one rule for both pipelines, for an agent's claim and a registry's alike (mcp_auto_discovery/secret_policy.py).  A name classed as a credential never keeps an inline value: its value is dropped and the entry carries a ${NAME} reference the operator exports.  Erring towards "secret" is not free either -- a variable wrongly classed ships a placeholder nobody can fill, and a server that needs the real value does not start. Whole words of a variable or header name that make it a credential.  Matched as UPPER_SNAKE words, never substrings: "auth" as a substring caught NODE_TLS_REJECT_UNAUTHORIZED, GIT_AUTHOR_NAME and AUTHORITY. "authorization" too: OPENQA_EXAMPLE_NET_AUTHORIZATION holds an Authorization header's value, and "auth" matches only as a whole word. |
| `selector_words` | `["mode", "type", "scheme", "method", "format", "style", "kind", "st…` | Last words that make a name a *choice* or an *identifier* rather than a secret, overriding the above: BUGZILLA_AUTH_MODE selects how to log in; a COMMIT, SHA or DIGEST names a revision -- random-looking, and not a secret. |
| `location_words` | `["sock", "socket", "file", "path", "dir", "directory"]` | Trailing words that make a variable a location -- where something is -- not a credential: SSH_AUTH_SOCK (an agent's socket), a key's *_KEY_FILE path. |
| `carrier_patterns` | `['(^\|_)HEADERS?$', '(^\|_)BASIC(_AUTH)?$']` | Names whose *shape* carries a credential, whatever words they use: a header list carries the Authorization header, a basic-auth value carries user:password.  build.example.net's login token sat under API_HEADERS, which no word above names, and was written into .mcp.json as a setting's default. Regular expressions, case-insensitive. |
| `inline_credential_patterns` | `[ …` | A credential carried inline in an argument, a URL or a header value (Bearer abc..., --token=abc..., ?api_key=abc...) -- whatever it is called. Regular expressions, matched case-insensitively. |
| `not_a_secret_words` | `["true", "false", "yes", "no", "on", "off", "none", "null"]` | Values that are configuration however the variable is named (SESSION_TIMEOUT=30 keeps its value): these words, and numbers of up to not_a_secret_max_digits digits. |
| `not_a_secret_max_digits` | `10` |  |
| `not_opaque_starts` | `["/", "./", "../", "~", "$", "{", "[", "\"", "'", "<", "-", "@"]` | A long random-looking value is a credential whatever its name (mcp.discovery.reuse.opaque_value_min_*) -- unless it starts like configuration: a path, a reference, a document, a flag, a scope. |
| `pasted_value_min_chars` | `24` | A run this long of anything but letters in a server's *description* of a variable is taken for a pasted credential, and the description dropped. |

### `[mcp.discovery]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `reuse_existing` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_REUSE_EXISTING:-true}"` | Offer this machine's existing registrations back as candidates (--no-reuse-existing-mcp turns it off).  A later run used to search from nothing while .mcp.json -- or `claude mcp add` -- already held a working entry for the very address asked about.  Each one matched to an address by host is verified, grounded and gated at its own tier like anything discovery found; a literal credential in it is never copied, only named.  See [mcp.discovery.reuse]. |
| `well_known_chars` | `1200` | Characters of JSON kept from each /.well-known document fetched, in the report's findings. 0 keeps everything. |
| `response_scan_chars` | `4000` | Characters of a reply's body searched for markers -- credential refusals, protocol hints, authentication evidence. A marker past this point is not seen. 0 searches the whole body. |
| `registry_remote_other_hosts` | `3` | How many *other* hostnames one official-registry answer may send us to probe. A registry `remotes[]` entry is the vendor saying where their MCP endpoint lives, and it very often is not on the hostname you typed: github.com is served from api.githubcopilot.com, developers.google.com from developerknowledge.googleapis.com.  Those URLs used to be dropped before they were probed, which cost a real server -- step D still recorded the endpoint, so the tier gate refused tiers 2-4 *because it exists*, and the address finished with nothing registered at all. So they are probed.  Whether one may be *registered* is decided afterwards by mcp_auto_discovery/grounding.py, which requires that it answered.  The cap is here because a registry answer is somebody else's data and should not be able to send an unbounded number of requests to hosts nobody asked about; 0 removes the cap, and on-host remotes are never capped. |
| `clients_install_missing` | `true` | Install a client a bridge drives when it is missing (each client's `install` in [mcp.discovery.clients.<name>]), before the bridge is trialled -- in both modes, for new and existing entries.  false leaves the bridge broken instead. |
| `provisional_settles_target` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_PROVISIONAL_SETTLES_TARGET:-true}"` | Whether an endpoint that answered by demanding a credential ends the tier descent, the way a working one does.  It should: since a package is trialled without its secret, "provisional" is the honest verdict for any target whose server wants a token, and treating only "verified" as an answer sent such a target on through the package and bridge stages -- minutes of agent time each, chasing a question already answered, and a second .mcp.json entry competing with the first.  Set false to keep searching lower tiers anyway. --exhaustive-mcp overrides this and never stops early. |
| `proven_replaces_unproved` | `true` | The descent continues past a verified tier only because nothing there proved access; a server below whose login a call accepted then takes the place of every server whose access was never proved -- one server per address, chosen by proof (off under --exhaustive-mcp, which keeps everything).  gitlab.example.net got efficient-gitlab (every call public) and its proven bridge, both written. |
| `offered_unproved_keeps_searching` | `true` | ...except a server given the credential this machine holds for the address that still proved nothing: it is not waiting for that credential, so it settles nothing (gitlab.example.net's mcp-graphql had the token its entry carried and no call could prove it). |
| `path_templates` | `[ …` | Candidate paths appended to the target base URL, tried in this order. Templates may contain {version}, expanded from version_segments below. |
| `sse_path_templates` | `[ …` | Paths probed as the deprecated HTTP+SSE transport (GET, text/event-stream). |
| `query_templates` | `["?format=mcp", "?transport=mcp", "?protocol=mcp"]` | Query-string forms: some gateways serve MCP off an ordinary route, selected by a parameter rather than by a path.  Each is appended to the origin and to every entry in query_bases, so "?format=mcp" covers both "https://host?format=mcp" and "https://host/api?format=mcp". |
| `query_bases` | `["", "/api", "/mcp"]` |  |
| `websocket_path_templates` | `["/ws", "/mcp/ws", "/{version}/ws", "/ws/mcp"]` | Paths checked for a WebSocket MCP transport.  Claude Code cannot speak WebSocket to an MCP server directly, so these are probed for *detection*: a 101 or 426 here is reported as a native endpoint that needs a bridge, which is a very different answer from "this host does not do MCP". |
| `websocket_requires_mcp_evidence` | `true` | An upgrade alone is not MCP: many services keep a WebSocket for their own pages (live job updates, notifications). With websocket_requires_mcp_evidence the upgrade counts as a native MCP endpoint -- one that closes the lower tiers and asks for a bridge -- only when the server accepts one of websocket_mcp_subprotocols (offered in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol) or the route matches one of websocket_mcp_path_patterns (regexes on the lowercased path). Anything else is reported as a hint and decides nothing. A refusal status (4xx/5xx) is never an upgrade, whatever headers come with it. |
| `websocket_mcp_subprotocols` | `["mcp"]` |  |
| `websocket_mcp_path_patterns` | `["(^\|/)mcp(/\|$)"]` |  |
| `version_segments` | `["v1", "v2", "v0", "api/v1", "1", "2"]` |  |
| `well_known_paths` | `[ …` | Standards-based hints. Only the OAuth ones are in the MCP specification; the others are widely deployed conventions worth a single cheap GET. |
| `api_spec_paths` | `[ …` | Machine-readable API descriptions used by stage 3 to synthesise a bridge. |
| `api_doc_pages` | `["/apidocs/", "/api-docs/", "/docs/", "/api/docs/", "/swagger-ui/",…` | Pages where a service documents its API for people -- Swagger UI, ReDoc -- read when no api_spec_path answered.  The description they render is found with the patterns below, in the page and in the scripts it loads. |
| `api_spec_link_patterns` | `[ …` | Regexes whose first group is a link to an API description.  Swagger UI names it in `url:` or `urls: [{url: ...}]`, ReDoc in `spec-url=`. |
| `api_doc_script_patterns` | `[ …` | Scripts a documentation page loads that may carry its configuration. |
| `api_doc_max_scripts` | `3` |  |
| `api_spec_same_host_only` | `true` | A description on another host is somebody else's API -- Swagger UI's own default points at a public demo -- so only the target's own host counts. |
| `extra_ports` | `[]` | Ports appended when the target is a bare host with no port. |
| `local_ports` | `[3000, 3001, 8000, 8080, 8081, 8787, 5000, 9000, 6274, 6277]` | Extra ports tried for loopback/private targets, where MCP servers usually run. |
| `scan_html` | `true` | Fetch the target's landing page and mine it for MCP links. |
| `html_link_patterns` | `[ …` | Multi-line literal strings: a regex here may contain both quote characters. |
| `stop_at_first` | `true` | Stop probing paths as soon as one endpoint answers.  Turned off automatically by --exhaustive-mcp, which is asked to find them all, and by --the-best-mcp, which cannot compare servers it never looked for. |
| `max_concurrency` | `8` | Concurrency and budget. |
| `target_concurrency` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_CONCURRENCY:-1}"` | How many *addresses* are worked at the same time (--concurrency N).  The keyword "bare" -- what bare --concurrency passes -- means target_concurrency_bare, below. 1 is strictly one after another, and is the default because it is the behaviour every run has always had: at 1 no thread is started and none of the machinery below executes at all. Phase 4 is ~98% agent thinking and addresses are independent of one another, so raising this is the only thing that meaningfully shortens a long run. It reduces *waiting*, not work: the same turns happen and the same tokens are spent, just overlapped. Three consequences worth knowing: * Each server's narration is held back and printed as one block, in the order the addresses were given, so two servers never interleave. * mcp.agent.max_budget_usd is applied when a target is *admitted* rather than inside a stage, so no target's agent loop is cut short by what another target spent -- the agent still owns its stage. * N model sessions at once provokes rate limiting, which is why a transient failure no longer consumes one of the agent's attempts (mcp.agent.transient_free_retries). Every address worked at once shares one pipeline, so whatever outlives one address is guarded: the agent workspace is prepared once, under a lock, and swapped into place whole; each address's agents write under their own artifacts/<address> directory; a retry that changes model or runtime changes it for that address only (the next address *starts* where the last change left off, as a one-at-a-time run always did); identical install steps are serialised; and one control probe per origin is shared, not raced.  A stage whose agent machinery raises is finished by the deterministic pipeline, as an exhausted agent loop is, instead of leaving the tiers below it closed. |
| `target_concurrency_bare` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_CONCURRENCY_BARE:-4}"` | What bare --concurrency (no number) means.  A setting, not a number in the parser, so it can be tuned to a backend's rate limits without a code change. |
| `per_request_timeout_seconds` | `8` |  |
| `stage_timeout_seconds` | `180` |  |
| `max_candidates` | `200` | Raised for the checklist: the mandated paths are emitted first and on every origin, so the cap can never be what quietly turned step A into a partial search. |
| `preflight` | `true` | Send a HEAD/GET reachability check before the JSON-RPC POST storm. |
| `tls_insecure_retry` | `true` | -- step B: transport and TLS bypasses -------------------------------------- A certificate this machine does not trust is a fact about the network -- a corporate middlebox, an internal CA, a self-signed dev server -- and not an answer to "does this host speak MCP".  So a TLS failure is retried once with verification off, and the endpoint that answers is reported as insecure rather than silently accepted: it is marked in the report, penalised in the ranking, and the operator is told to install the CA certificate. |
| `tls_error_markers` | `[ …` | Substrings that identify a failure as a certificate problem rather than an absent server.  Matched case-insensitively against the transport error; the wording comes from whichever TLS stack is installed, so it is configurable. |
| `try_both_schemes` | `true` | Probe http:// as well as https:// for every host, not only for loopback. Plenty of internal services are plaintext-only. |
| `strip_auth_on_cleartext` | `true` | Never send the configured bearer token over cleartext http to a non-local host: a probe must not be the thing that leaks the credential.  The probe still happens, without the header. |
| `cleartext_stripped_headers` | `["authorization", "proxy-authorization", "cookie", "x-api-key"]` |  |
| `protocol_hint_headers` | `[ …` | -- step C: handshake headers and response hints ---------------------------- Response headers read for evidence of an MCP-ish protocol even when the handshake itself failed: an SSE content type, a WebSocket upgrade, an OAuth challenge, a session id.  Lower-case names. |
| `protocol_hint_markers` | `["jsonrpc", "protocolversion", "mcp-session-id", "notifications/ini…` | Substrings looked for in a response *body* that say "JSON-RPC lives here" even when the reply was an error: a JSON-RPC envelope, an MCP method name. |
| `reply_excerpt_chars` | `160` | What a rejection records about the reply it rejected: status, content type and this many characters of the body, redacted.  "not a JSON-RPC message" on its own says nothing about *what* came back, which is the one thing needed to tell a proxy's placeholder from a real refusal.  0 records no body at all. |
| `inconclusive_retries` | `1` | A 2xx that is neither a refusal nor JSON-RPC proves nothing either way, so it is asked again this many times, this far apart, before it is recorded -- as "inconclusive", never as "this URL does not speak MCP". |
| `inconclusive_retry_delay_seconds` | `1` |  |
| `api_kinds_same_host_only` | `true` | API kinds other than an OpenAPI document -- see [mcp.discovery.api_kinds.*] below.  Only a page on the target's own host may name the endpoint, for the reason api_spec_same_host_only gives. |
| `api_kind_adapter_confidence` | `0.7` | Ordering hint for a generic server of an API kind (an adapter below) that sets no confidence of its own; verification is what decides. |
| `api_kind_min_shared_tools` | `2` | A bridge -- an agent's or anybody's -- serves a detected API kind when at least this many of its tools are named as the kind's documented operations (all of them, for a kind that lists fewer), or a launch value names the kind's own path on the target.  It is then judged as that kind's bridge ("a proven alternative"), whoever wrote it and whether or not it said so: sd.example.com's agent bridge served the customer API without saying so, and an unchecked package kept the address. |
| `api_kind_control_name` | `"initialize-claude-ai-control"` | The control request: once a path is recognised, the same request is sent to a sibling whose last segment is this name, which cannot exist.  If that is recognised too, the server answers everything that way and the kind is not recognised.  "" switches the control off. |
| `api_kinds_behind_login` | `true` | A kind (or a catalogue product, mcp.discovery.auth.recognise_behind_login) whose own path answers 401/403 in an API's form -- not a web page -- while a sibling that cannot exist is answered otherwise, is there behind a login.  sd.example.com came to refuse /rest/servicedeskapi/info and /rest/api/2/serverInfo to anonymous callers; detection read only a 2xx, and nothing downstream saw the customer API or the Jira behind it. |
| `api_kind_bridge_when_generic_fails` | `true` | A kind with generic servers (adapters) is theirs first; this program's own bridge from the kind's operations backs them up once they were tried for the address -- by any stage or agent -- and none passed.  gitlab.example.net's mcp-graphql could not reach it from Node, and the address ended with nothing. |
| `generated_bridge_settles_first` | `true` | Before the bridge stage is skipped or ended, the bridge generated from a detected API kind's documented operations (`operations` below) is tried, unless something has already *proved* access -- an accepted login, or a server that works with nothing left unproved.  A server only waiting for a credential, or one refused by an agent's own bridge, proves nothing: sd.example.com's agent-written bridge ended the bridge stage, and the bridge generated from the documented operations was never built.  Applies to both modes; candidates are then ranked by proof, not by which arrived first. |
| `identify_retries` | `2` | Identifying the address -- its product, its login challenges, its API kinds -- is asked again identify_retries times (after login_check.temporary_retry_seconds) when the server answers "try again later" (login_check.temporary_statuses). Still undecided, nothing unproven settles the address: sd.example.com answered 502, its customer API went undetected, and a waiting mcp-atlassian closed the bridge stage. |
| `undecided_keeps_searching` | `true` |  |
| `reidentify_undecided` | `true` | Each retry waits what the host asked for (Retry-After) or a pause that doubles per attempt, capped by login_check.temporary_retry_max_seconds.  An address still undecided is identified again the next time its login plan is asked for (reidentify_undecided), and meanwhile takes the product it was when it last answered (remembered_product_when_busy): bugzilla.opensuse.org answered 429, came out "product unknown; logins offered: none seen", and nothing asked what it logs in with. |
| `reidentify_times` | `1` |  |
| `reidentify_after_seconds` | `60` |  |
| `remembered_product_when_busy` | `true` |  |
