### `[mcp.discovery.reuse]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `manifest_login_slots` | `true` | Each login variable a generated bridge's manifest declares (a client bridge's parts, a bridge's auth.variables), still empty, is a credential to supply when its entry is read back -- credential-looking name or not: osc signing needs only the user name, and build-example-net's signing bridge, read back without it as a credential, was refused and lost to a password bridge. |
| `sources` | `["project_file", "claude_cli"]` | Where existing registrations are read from: "project_file" is the .mcp.json this phase writes (mcp.mcp_json_path), "claude_cli" is what mcp.registration.list_command / get_command report (user and local scope). |
| `claude_config` | `"{config_dir}/.claude.json"` | The claude CLI's entries are read from Claude Code's own configuration -- user scope and this project's local scope -- exactly as kept: `claude mcp get` prints ${NAME:-default} as ${NAME}, and build-example-net's working entry was judged "${ICA_MCP_PYTHON3_13} is not installed" from that print. {config_dir} is $<claude_config_dir_variable> when set, else the home directory. |
| `claude_config_dir_variable` | `"CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR"` |  |
| `connected_outranks_trial` | `true` | An entry `claude mcp list` reports connected is never judged "does not start" by this run's own launch, and is replaced only by a server that proved it does the job. |
| `check_manifests` | `true` | A generated bridge's entry and the manifest it names must agree on the variables its login reads; one that disagrees (a manifest rewritten for another route) is broken, and replaced -- never "waiting for a credential" it is never passed. |
| `repair_missing_slots` | `true` | An existing entry whose only fault is a slot its manifest reads and it does not pass gets the slot back (${NAME:-}) and stays -- it is not replaced: build-example-net lost BUILD_EXAMPLE_NET_USERNAME in one run and was kept that way. |
| `refresh_generated_scripts` | `true` | An existing entry running an older copy of a bridge this program generates (recognised by the template's first lines, its manifest of a schema the current template reads) has the script refreshed in place before it is tried: template fixes reach kept entries too.  Never in a dry run. |
| `recheck_when_blocked` | `true` | A stage the tier policy closes (a native endpoint was found) still re-checks this machine's existing registrations at that tier, so a working entry is compared with what closed it rather than hidden by it: smelt.example.net's connected mcp-graphql was never looked at once another host's endpoint closed the package stage, and was replaced by it.  No new package or bridge is searched for; only what is already registered here is judged. |
| `recheck_when_settled_unproven` | `true` | ...and so does a stage skipped because a server that only waits for a credential settled the descent: nothing proved that one, so it cannot hide what is already here.  gitlab.example.net's package stage found mcp-graphql waiting for a token; the bridge Claude Code showed connected (the entry that last worked) sat in the bridge tier, was never looked at, and was replaced. When the re-checked entry works, the unproven one gives its place up. |
| `give_held_credentials` | `true` | An existing or remembered copy of an API-kind adapter that takes no credential, while the address holds one, is given it the way the adapter declares (credential_env) before it is judged: a copy proved on anonymous calls alone had been recorded as working and kept the token-carrying entry out. |
| `credential_in_taken_form` | `true` | ...also one whose credential key holds a single bare reference, which the operator would have to fill with the whole form: the agent proposed mcp-graphql with HEADERS = ${GITLAB_EXAMPLE_NET_HEADERS:-} (a JSON object nobody exports; empty, the server exited at start-up) and the held token was never given.  Every written entry gets the adapter's form around a variable holding the credential itself -- the held one, else credential_variable ({SLUG} = the entry's name in upper case).  A variable that already has a value where Claude Code runs is the operator's whole value and is kept. |
| `credential_variable` | `"{SLUG}_TOKEN"` |  |
| `slot_when_short_of_login` | `true` | An adapter's copy with no credential slot at all, that answered while a usage task needing the account failed, is given the slot -- optional, in the adapter's form -- so the login has somewhere to go.  gitlab-example-net was kept with no HEADERS, every call anonymous, and the token had nowhere to go.  The entry is still started as written, so a server that minds the empty form is caught there. |
| `worked_before_wins` | `true` | Between two candidates that proved equally little, the one known to have worked on this machine -- the entry that last passed here (mcp.known_good), or the copy Claude Code loads and shows connected -- keeps its place. |
| `connected_counts_as_worked` | `false` | Being connected in Claude Code is not working: a server connects and can still fail every call (sd.example.com's mcp-atlassian).  Off, only the entry that last passed here (mcp.known_good) counts as having worked; on, a connected CLI copy counts too. |
| `keep_operator_references` | `true` | A setting an existing entry wrote as a reference (${BUILD_OPENSUSE_ORG_USERNAME}) is expanded to launch the trial and written back as that reference -- never as the value: the expansion put the operator's user name into .mcp.json. This program's own path variables are derived again from the path instead. |
| `keep_instance_literal` | `true` | ...except a value that names a host: it says which instance the entry serves, and a reference to a generic variable (BUGZILLA_SERVER, exported in the operator's shell for bugzilla.opensuse.org) would make the entry serve whatever that variable says tomorrow -- two instances of one product cannot both own it. Such a value stays in the entry (an existing reference to one is written back as its value), unless the variable is namespaced to the entry. |
| `confidence` | `0.9` | Ordering hint for a reused candidate; verification is what decides. |
| `bridge_patterns` | `[]` | A local entry is a bridge (tier 3) when its launch line matches mcp.bridge.generated.filename_template, or one of these regular expressions; any other local entry is a package (tier 2), and a remote one an endpoint. |
| `literal_env_template` | `"{NAME}_{KEY}"` | A literal credential found in an entry is replaced by a reference to this variable.  {NAME} is the entry's name, {KEY} the variable or header it was in, both upper-cased with "_" for punctuation. |
| `paths_are_settings` | `true` | A value that is an absolute path -- as written, or every reference's default -- is where the server finds something (a key file, a bundle), not the secret itself: an existing entry is trialled with it, as Claude Code launches it. build-example-net's ${..._OBS_SSH_KEY:-/root/.ssh/id_ed25519} was withheld as a credential, its SSH-signing bridge could not log in, and a server that never could took its place. |
| `opaque_value_min_chars` | `24` | A literal is also a credential when it *looks* like one, whatever the variable is called: a single token at least opaque_value_min_chars long, with letters and digits, at least opaque_value_min_entropy bits of entropy per character, and not a URL, path, ${reference}, JSON document or file name.  A 44-character base64 token under SMELT_EXAMPLE_NET_HEADERS was once copied from a CLI registration into .mcp.json because "HEADERS" is not a secret word.  Such a value is never copied; the entry references an exported variable instead. |
| `opaque_value_min_entropy` | `4.0` |  |
| `opaque_value_min_entropy_ratio` | `0.85` | ...or this share of the most the value's own alphabet allows (hex, lower alphanumeric, alphanumeric, base64, printable): 32 random hex digits carry at most 4 bits each, so the absolute threshold alone called a hex token not random.  0 turns the relative test off. |
| `list_line_pattern` | `'^(?P<name>[^\s:]+):\s.+\s-\s'` | How a `claude mcp list` line names its server. |
| `expand_from_claude_settings` | `true` | The scopes `claude mcp get` reports for an entry that lives in the project's .mcp.json: that is the file's own entry, never a CLI copy -- no check calls it "a different copy that takes precedence", and nothing removes it as one. Anchored at the start: "Local config (private to you in this project)" says "project" too, and is a CLI copy. An existing entry's ${NAME} is read as Claude Code expands it: the environment, then Claude Code's settings env, then the default -- and for this program's own ICA_MCP_* variable whose default is not on this machine, what it stands for here.  github-com was judged "not installed" while the settings named the binary that is here. |
| `project_scope_patterns` | `['(?i)^\s*project\b', '(?i)\.mcp\.json']` |  |

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `type` | `"Type"` |  |

| `args` | `"Args"` |  |
| `url` | `"URL"` |  |
| `env` | `"Environment"` |  |
| `headers` | `"Headers"` |  |
| `scope` | `"Scope"` | "Scope: Project config (shared via .mcp.json)": the file's own entry, which `claude mcp get` reports too -- never a copy the CLI holds (see mcp.discovery.reuse.project_scope_patterns). |

### `[mcp.discovery.auth]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `claim_needs_control` | `true` | A claim that a URL wants a credential (an agent's, an auth profile's) is credited to an inconclusive reply only when that reply differs from what a made-up path on the same host gets (control_probe).  confluence.example.com redirected /mcp to its login page exactly as it redirects a path that does not exist. |
| `reask_unreachable_origin` | `true` | An origin that did not answer the first probe is asked once more before the login plan is made; still silent, the plan is made from the challenges it gave before (remember_challenges).  build.example.net timed out once under --concurrency and got no plan at all. |
| `read_challenges` | `true` | Read every login challenge of the target and its API hosts, recognise the product, and choose how to log in (see [mcp.discovery.auth.methods] and [mcp.discovery.products.*]).  A scoped, revocable token first, then a key and secret, then a user name and password -- what an operator holds -- and a login only a client performs (signing with an SSH key, Kerberos) last: an operator may have no key registered, and build.example.net offers a password login beside api.example.net's Signature.  {domain} = the registrable domain. |
| `instance_bound_patterns` | `['(^\|_)(TOKEN\|PAT\|API_?KEY\|KEY\|SECRET\|BEARER)($\|_)']` | A token or an API key is issued by one server, so the same one in entries for two different servers is reported (names matching these patterns).  A user name and password is never reported for that: the same one may work on many servers (single sign-on), and a server that refuses it says so itself. |
| `methods_equal` | `true` | Every kind of login counts the same -- an SSH-key signature, a token, a key and secret, a user name and password: whatever makes the server fully work wins, by proof (a call that needs the login accepted, its usage checks passed, a new terminal's Claude Code uses it).  Before anything is proved, logins are ordered by evidence only -- what this host accepted or refused before, which logins its API host itself offers, what this machine holds -- never by kind.  With methods_equal on, method_order is only the order alternatives are listed in; off, it decides again (token, then key and secret, password, client login). |
| `method_order` | `["token", "apikey", "basic", "client"]` |  |
| `offered_only_methods` | `["basic"]` | Methods chosen only when a challenge seen on the target or its API hosts offered them: a password login is advertised in its 401, a token or a key usually is not.  api.example.net offers only Signature, so no password is chosen there. |
| `try_unoffered_methods` | `true` | ...where "offered" includes proof by trying: a challenge names what a service advertises, not all it accepts (sd.example.com's 401 says OAuth; its API takes a user name and password).  Each method above the challenge left out is sent once as a stand-in nobody owns to a read that needs a login; an answer that differs from the anonymous one counts as offered. |
| `api_host_patterns` | `["api.{domain}"]` |  |
| `api_host_same_product` | `true` | An API host guessed from the name counts only when it is recognised as the same catalogue product as the target -- api.example.net is build.example.net's, not gitlab.example.net's or smelt.example.net's; api.example.com is not sd.example.com's. |
| `recognise_behind_login` | `true` | A product whose recognition path asks for a login (in its API's form, a control path answered otherwise) is recognised behind that login, when no product answered openly -- see mcp.discovery.api_kinds_behind_login. |
| `prefer_held_methods` | `true` | A method the operator already holds credentials for comes first -- their own for the address, then (basic only) one held for another address of the same organisation -- before method_order decides among the rest. |
| `prefer_in_use_methods` | `true` | The kind of credential an existing entry already sends this host -- a token in sd.example.com's mcp-atlassian entry -- counts as held: the generated server asks for that kind, and is offered that value, before another address's login is tried (sd.example.com's bridge had been given build.example.net's password login). |
| `prefer_detected_api` | `true` | Between two servers waiting for a credential, neither of which proved access, the one built for an API kind this host was seen to serve (a detected API, open or behind its login) takes the slot from one that is not: sd.example.com serves a Service Management customer API that jira.example.com does not, and mcp-atlassian -- whose calls a customer account is sent to the portal for -- kept the slot over the bridge for that API.  Proof always decides first. |
| `challenge_paths` | `["/"]` |  |
| `bearer_token_ref` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_TOKEN_REF:-}"` |  |
| `header_name` | `"Authorization"` |  |
| `header_template` | `"Bearer {token}"` |  |
| `register_authenticated` | `true` | An endpoint that answers 401 or 403 has proved it exists and speaks to authenticated clients.  That is a find, not a dead end, so it is written into .mcp.json with its credential slot left empty -- ${NAME}, never a value -- and reported as needing one.  Turn this off to go back to recording such an endpoint in the report only. |
| `require_mcp_evidence` | `true` | ...but only when the rejection looked like a protocol answer. A 401 is a find on a host that mostly answers 200.  On a Jira, a Confluence, a service desk or any intranet it is the answer to *every* URL, including paths that do not exist -- so there the status says nothing about MCP, and believing it registers the website as a server.  No credential can make that entry work, which is the worst kind of wrong answer: it looks like progress and sends the operator hunting for a token that would not have helped. The test is deliberately generous, because discarding a real endpoint is the worse mistake: any ONE of the signals below is enough, and only an HTML login page with nothing else to say fails it.  false restores the older behaviour, where a bare 401 was taken at face value. |
| `evidence_headers` | `["Mcp-Session-Id", "MCP-Protocol-Version"]` | Headers that only an MCP endpoint would put on a rejection. |
| `evidence_challenge_markers` | `["resource_metadata", "mcp"]` | Substrings in WWW-Authenticate that point at the MCP/OAuth resource discovery flow rather than at a website's login. |
| `evidence_body_markers` | `["jsonrpc", "\"error\":{\"code\"", "protocolVersion"]` | Substrings in the response body that mean a protocol spoke, not a page. |
| `disqualifying_content_types` | `["text/html", "application/xhtml+xml"]` | Content types that are a web page and therefore not, on their own, evidence of anything.  Any other content type counts as evidence: a bare JSON or plain text 401 from an API gateway is still an API answering. |
| `control_probe` | `true` | The negative control, and the only check here that needs to know nothing about the product on the other end. "This endpoint wants a credential" is a claim about *this* URL, and it only holds on a host where not everything answers the same way.  So before trusting a refusal, ask a path that cannot exist: if the invented path is refused identically, the refusal was the site's habit and says nothing about MCP. This is what generalises.  A list of products whose 401s are meaningless needs a new entry for every Jira, Confluence, service desk and intranet ever deployed; a control probe costs one request per origin, is cached for the run, and works on hosts nobody has heard of.  It also catches what the content-type rule above cannot: a gateway that answers every path with the same JSON error. |
| `control_path_template` | `"/initialize-claude-ai-control-{nonce}"` |  |
| `header_schemes` | `["Bearer", "Basic", "Token", "ApiKey"]` | Schemes worth copying out of a WWW-Authenticate challenge and into the entry. Jira advertises `OAuth realm="..."` -- that is OAuth 1.0a, its legacy application-link mechanism, and a personal access token is NOT sent that way: it is a Bearer token.  Sending `Authorization: OAuth <PAT>` produces a second 401 the operator then has to diagnose.  A scheme not on this list falls back to header_template above, with a note saying what the server asked for. |
| `token_env_template` | `"{SLUG}_TOKEN"` | How the empty slot is named when nothing better named one: neither the discovering agent (which may have read the vendor's documentation) nor bearer_token_ref above.  {SLUG} is the server's own name, upper-cased, so gitlab-example-net asks for GITLAB_EXAMPLE_NET_TOKEN -- recognisably that service's, and not a generic name the next authenticated target would collide with. |
| `shape_separators` | `[":", "/", "\|"]` | Products whose credential is not a single opaque token, and what theirs actually looks like. "Export OPENQA_OPENSUSE_ORG_TOKEN" is only useful advice where the product issues something called a token.  Where it does not, the operator is sent looking for a thing that does not exist -- so the exceptions are recorded here rather than guessed at.  Each entry matches a host and may set: match   regex, matched against the endpoint's hostname (required) env     variable name to use instead of token_env_template; {SLUG} works format  what the value looks like, printed with the variable name obtain  where to get one; {host} is substituted header_template  overrides the default "Bearer {token}" for this product Nothing here is a credential, and nothing here is required: a target with no matching entry gets the generic name, which is right for most of them. How a composite shape becomes a variable name.  "username:key:secret" gives <SLUG>_USERNAME_KEY_SECRET, so the name *is* the instruction and an operator cannot read it as "set the key".  A shape with no separator is a single opaque token and keeps the ordinary naming, where "..._TOKEN" is both accurate and shorter. |
| `shape_max_parts` | `4` |  |
| `spec_value_patterns` | `['\.(ya?ml\|json)(\?\|$)', '/(openapi\|swagger\|apidocs?)(/\|\b)']` | Phrases that mean "a human should log in here", which overrule every piece of evidence above rather than adding to them.  The generosity of the evidence test rests on one clause -- "it answered application/json, not a web page" -- which is true of every JSON API and therefore of every JSON *error*. confluence.example.com answers an anonymous POST with {"errorMessage":"You are not logged in. <a href=\"/login.action\">Log in</a>"} and was registered as an MCP endpoint on the strength of it.  No MCP endpoint has any reason to say these things, so finding one is decisive.  Matched case-insensitively against the first 4000 bytes of the body. Only login *language*, never HTML structure.  "<form" and "<a href" were here and had to come out: they are markers of a web page, not of a login page, and disqualifying_content_types already handles HTML-ness.  Any API whose error body happens to contain a link would have had its evidence cleared -- a silent way to lose a real endpoint, which is exactly the failure this list exists to prevent in the other direction. A candidate's env value or argument that is a URL to an API description (OPENAPI_SPEC_PATH=https://build.example.net/apidocs/OBS-v2.10.50.yaml).  When a value does not fit its slot (value_shapes), the description's security scheme says how the service takes a credential, so the remedy can give the exact form. |
| `login_page_markers` | `[ …` |  |
| `max_provisional` | `1` | How many credential-walled endpoints are worth registering for one target.  A host that sits entirely behind a login answers 401 on every path probed; one entry for the best-ranked of them is a lead, a dozen is noise.  This is a budget for the whole target, spent across every stage that runs -- as a per-stage cap it was no cap at all, and jira.example.com came out of a default run with one entry from the package stage and another from the bridge stage. --exhaustive-mcp overrides it and keeps them all. (This key sat indented under the openqa profile below until 0.1.1, so nothing ever read it and the limit was whatever the call site passed as a default. A setting that no test asserts the *location* of is a setting that can move without anyone noticing -- see tests/test_mcp_settings_reachable.py.) |
| `credential_refusal_statuses` | `[200, 201, 202, 400, 406, 422]` | Refusals that do not come as a 401 or 403.  Some endpoints answer 200 or 400 with `{"error":"no api key"}` or "invalid personal access token"; for the statuses listed, a body carrying one of these markers is read as "a credential is required" -- and must still pass the evidence test above (the control probe and login_page_markers included) before it is an MCP endpoint. |
| `credential_refusal_markers` | `[ …` |  |
| `credit_inconclusive_with_claim` | `true` | An *inconclusive* anonymous reply (a 2xx that is not JSON-RPC) from a URL that somebody has good reason to believe wants a credential is registered provisionally, exactly like a 401 with evidence: an empty ${VAR} slot named by the auth profile.  The reasons that count -- each in words, never a value: * the candidate's own claim (an agent that read the product's documentation and proposed it with requires_auth, or the checklist that recorded it behind an auth wall) -- credit_inconclusive_with_claim; * an auth profile below matching the host: the operator has already said this product takes a credential -- profile_is_auth_claim. |
| `profile_is_auth_claim` | `true` |  |
| `remember_challenges` | `true` | Which login each host accepted or refused, kept run after run (with an account fingerprint, never a name or value): a scheme accepted before is tried first, one refused and never accepted for this account last -- before what is held and before method_order.  build.example.net refused the password login every run, and every run tried it first. A login challenge a host gave in an earlier run counts when it gives none in this one (no answer, a 503 while it was recognised), for this many days: api.opensuse.org's Basic went missing once and the plan could not tell the client bridge's login from a proxy's unknown one.  Stored in the state folder. |

### `[mcp.discovery.auth.evidence]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | With nothing proved, what the run knows breaks the tie -- never list order or an agent's confidence: a scheme this host refused before goes last; the one the address's API host itself asks for, and the one needing fewer values the operator has not supplied, come first.  build.example.net's run wrote a password bridge over the SSH-key route its own plan had chosen. |
| `scheme_patterns` | `{ basic = ["PASSWORD$", "PASSWD$", "_PASS$"], signature = ["SSH_KEY…` | A candidate that names no scheme is told by the slots it reads -- credential or setting: a key file's path is a setting, and it still says the server signs (build.example.net's SSH-signing bridge read OBS_SSH_KEY and was ranked "unknown" beside a header proxy that could never log in). |
| `value_schemes` | `{ bearer = ['\bbearer\b'], basic = ['\bbasic\b'] }` | ...and first by the form a slot's value takes ("Authorization:Bearer ${…}" is a bearer login whatever the slot is called -- EXTRA_HEADERS promises nothing). |
| `method_schemes` | `{ token = ["bearer", "token"], apikey = ["bearer", "token", "apikey…` | The schemes the login plan's chosen method stands for: a product that takes tokens often advertises only OAuth and Basic in its challenge (Jira's personal access tokens are sent as Bearer), so a chosen "token" counts them as offered. |
| `unoffered_last` | `true` | A candidate whose scheme the address offers nowhere it was asked goes after every candidate whose scheme is offered or unknown. |
| `unknown_below_offered` | `true` | A candidate whose login is of no known kind ranks below one whose kind the address offers -- before "values still to supply" decides anything. build-opensuse-org's proxy (one value, unknown kind) outranked the client bridge (user name and password, the Basic login the address offers). |
| `host_matters` | `true` | The login the API host asks for counts only when it is sent there: a candidate whose URL settings (or, failing those, a file it names) point at another host ranks as "offered elsewhere".  build-opensuse-org's agent bridge sent Basic to build.opensuse.org (refused); the osc bridge's manifest says apiurl = https://api.opensuse.org (accepted); both had counted as "asked at the API host". |
| `count_header_credentials` | `true` | A credential a URL entry sends in a header is a value to supply too: a URL waiting for `Bearer ${TOKEN}` listed nothing pending and won "fewer values" against a server needing the same one token. |
| `client_bridge_is_built_for_api` | `true` | A bridge driving the product's own client (osc) is built for the address's API as much as one generated from its API kind: build-example-net's password bridge (OBS kind) outranked the osc bridge signing at api.example.net -- the only login that API accepts -- before the logins were compared. |
| `client_bridge_markers` | `["MCP_CLIENT_MANIFEST"]` |  |
| `url_setting_keys` | `['(^\|_)(BASE_)?URL$', '(^\|_)API(_URL\|_BASE\|_HOST)?$', '(^\|_)ENDPOIN…` |  |
| `url_assignment_pattern` | `'''(?i)\b(?:api_?url\|base_?url\|endpoint\|server_?url)\b\s*[=:]\s*["'…` |  |
| `one_comparison` | `true` | One comparison for every chooser -- the per-stage pick, the cross-stage slot, an existing entry keeping its place -- by what is known (proof, history, the API a candidate is built for, the login the address asks for), never by tier order or confidence alone.  sd.example.com's earliest stage kept a core-Jira server over the bridge for the customer API it was seen to serve. |

### `[mcp.packages]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `search_timeout_seconds` | `"${cfg:http.timeout_seconds}"` | How long one registry search may take; the general HTTP timeout unless set. |
| `registry_url` | `"https://registry.modelcontextprotocol.io"` | Official MCP registry (verified live: returns {servers:[{server:{...}}]}). |
| `registry_search_path` | `"/v0/servers?search={query}&limit={limit}"` |  |
| `npm_search_url` | `"https://registry.npmjs.org/-/v1/search?text={query}&size={limit}"` |  |
| `generic_host_labels` | `[ …` | Host labels that name no product, removed before a target becomes a search term.  The product is the *leftmost* meaningful label, because an internal host is <product>.<organisation>.<tld>: confluence.example.com is asked about as "confluence" (then "example"), not as "example". This list is load-bearing.  With ".de" missing from it, smelt.example.net was searched for as the single word "de" -- which is Spanish -- and npm answered with a Colombian regulatory-compliance server that was then registered as SMELT's MCP endpoint.  confluence.example.com and jira.example.com were both asked about as "example", so confluence-datacenter-mcp and jira-datacenter-mcp could never be found at all. |
| `require_relevance` | `true` | A package must have something to do with the target.  A registry search is a keyword match, and an unjudged keyword match answers "which server talks to Confluence?" with a TypeScript code generator -- @kubb/mcp was registered for bugzilla, confluence AND build.opensuse.org, because all three searches were keyword matches and it handshakes. Two ways to be relevant, and a gate that knows only the first is worse than none: the package names the product, OR it is a generic server configured for this host.  The second clause is what keeps mcp-graphql pointed at smelt.example.net -- a working entry that a name-only filter would discard. Rejections are listed in the report, so the rule can be argued with. "Names the product" means a whole word, a host label or a registry owner -- never a substring.  "example" inside "examplep_administradores" once made a Brazilian regulator's tool on api.mcp.ai "relevant" to six Example hosts. |
| `hosting_namespaces` | `["io.github", "io.gitlab", "io.bitbucket", "org.codeberg"]` | Official-registry namespaces that name an *account on a hosting service*, not a domain the publisher proved they own.  "io.github.mcp-dir/some-server" was published by the GitHub account "mcp-dir"; the word "github" in it says nothing about GitHub, so it is neither relevance to github.com nor GitHub vouching for the endpoint.  Every other namespace is read as reverse DNS -- "com.googleapis.developerknowledge/mcp" is Google's.  Used by the relevance gate here and by the registration grounding rule, in both modes.  Add a hosting service's reverse-DNS prefix here when the registry starts using it. |
| `trial_without_secrets` | `true` | Trial a package whose credential is not available, instead of refusing to launch it.  A stdio server reads its credential when a *tool is called*, so one trialled without it still completes the handshake and still advertises everything it can do: confluence-datacenter-mcp lists 115 tools with no token at all.  Refusing to start it is what let an irrelevant package that needed no credential win instead -- the candidate was punished for declaring its own requirements.  Such a server is registered provisionally, with the slot empty, exactly like an endpoint that answered 401; it is never counted as working. |
| `credential_wall_needs_tools` | `true` | ...but a server that starts and then advertises NOTHING is not a credential wall, and must not be recorded as one. The reason the trial above is worth doing is that a stdio server reads its credential when a tool is *called*, so one launched without it still lists everything it can do -- which is far more than refusing to start it teaches. With an empty capability list that whole justification is absent: we learned nothing, and nothing points at the credential as the reason. Guessing anyway costs the target. `mcp-atlassian` for confluence.example.com handshaked, listed zero tools, and was filed as "a real MCP endpoint that refused an anonymous client".  That made it provisional, which settled the target, which closed tiers 3 and 4 -- and shipped an entry naming `PERSONAL_TOKEN`, a variable that package does not read.  Supplying it changed nothing, because the credential was never the missing piece. An empty list has several causes and a missing token is only one: a variable named wrongly, a base URL the server rejected, a required argument nobody passed.  Left unaccepted, `accepts()` says the true thing -- "server exposes no tools, resources or prompts" -- and the lower tiers get their turn. false restores the older behaviour of treating any successful handshake with a missing secret as a credential wall. |
| `pypi_package_url` | `"https://pypi.org/pypi/{name}/json"` |  |
| `pypi_name_templates` | `[ …` | PyPI answers about one exact distribution name, not a query, so the names to ask about are produced here from the product name in {target}.  Each is normalised (PEP 503) before it is looked up.  Keep every template MCP-specific: a bare "{target}" would match an unrelated package that happens to share the product's name.  An empty list turns the PyPI route off, as does an empty pypi_package_url. |
| `pypi_max_lookups` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_PYPI_LOOKUPS:-6}"` | Ceiling on the lookups one target may cost, however long the list above is. |
| `github_search_url` | `"https://api.github.com/search/repositories?q={query}&per_page={lim…` |  |
| `github_token_ref` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_GITHUB_TOKEN_REF:-env:GITHUB_TOKEN}"` | Reference to a GitHub token; raises the 60/hour anonymous rate limit. |
| `query_templates` | `[ …` | Query templates for the full-text searches (npm, GitHub); {target} is the product name taken from the hostname. |
| `registry_query_templates` | `["{target}"]` | ...and for the official MCP registry, which is NOT a full-text search: its `search` parameter matches a substring of the server's *name*.  Verified live for confluence.example.com: "confluence mcp server" and "mcp-server-confluence" each returned 0 servers after 13-15 s (and so hit the 15 s timeout on a slower network), while "confluence" returned 10 in 7 s -- among them @atlassian-dc-mcp/confluence and confluence-datacenter-mcp, the two servers that target needed.  Every template above is a phrase no server name contains, so the registry, the one source with launch commands and declared variables, was contributing nothing.  The bare product tokens are always asked after these, as for the other sources. |
| `registry_timeout_seconds` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_REGISTRY_TIMEOUT:-30}"` | How long one official-registry request may take.  Separate from search_timeout_seconds because the registry is measurably slower than npm and a timeout there costs the best-structured source there is.  A timeout or an error from any source is reported in the stage's findings, not only in the debug log, so "no package matched" can be told apart from "nobody answered". |
| `limit` | `10` |  |
| `trial_run` | `true` | Try running a discovered package to see whether it really speaks MCP. |
| `check_launcher_usable` | `true` | Before a trial, the catalog component behind the launch program is asked whether it works here (its `purpose = "usable"` checks in 10-components.toml, once per run, shared with phase 1).  One that does not -- Docker with its daemon stopped -- is not launched: no verdict on the server, and the reason with its fix.  gitlab.example.net's container candidate was rejected as "not accepted" for want of a running daemon. |
| `sandbox_install` | `true` | Install into a throwaway directory rather than globally. |
| `sandbox_dir` | `"${cfg:paths.work_dir}/mcp-trials"` |  |
| `trial_timeout_seconds` | `90` |  |
| `slow_start_retries` | `1` | An *existing* registration that answered nothing within the trial deadline is tried again, this many times, each with the deadline multiplied by slow_start_timeout_factor, before "does not start" may replace it.  A first launch that downloads (uvx, npx) can outlast the deadline: sd.example.com's mcp-atlassian took 93 s once after starting in about a second on every earlier run, and was replaced.  A timeout alone also never replaces an entry `claude mcp list` reports connected.  0 retries none. |
| `slow_start_timeout_factor` | `2.0` |  |
| `failure_excerpt_chars` | `300` | How much of a failed trial's own words (its last stderr lines, redacted) the log and the agent's retry brief carry.  "failed without X" with nothing after it sent the reader to rerun the package by hand to find out why.  0 = none. |
| `provision_missing` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_PROVISION_MISSING:-auto}"` | --mcp-provision-missing: what happens when a local candidate's launch command or install step names a program that is not installed here. auto    install it from phase 1's catalog (10-components.toml) when that needs no password prompt -- root, a sudo/doas that answers without one, or a user-level strategy -- then trial the candidate as usual always  the same, trying every catalog strategy, privileged ones included never   do not install; the candidate is rejected as not installed true/false are accepted for always/never. Only catalog strategies ever run: a command a candidate or an agent wrote never causes an install. Each program is tried once per run, whatever the outcome, and what was installed or failed is in the report. It never changes which server is chosen: a program it cannot install is rejected in exactly the words it always was. |
| `provision_privilege_probe` | `["true"]` | Appended to the sudo/doas prefix to learn, without a prompt, whether privileged strategies can run in 'auto'. |
| `provision_privilege_probe_timeout_seconds` | `10` |  |
| `pin_versions` | `true` | A generic server offered for an API kind (mcp.discovery.api_kinds) is pinned to the version its registry calls current when the run starts, so the entry written is the launch that was trialled -- not whatever "latest" means on the day Claude Code next starts it.  false launches the bare package name. |
| `version_lookup_timeout_seconds` | `"${cfg:http.timeout_seconds}"` |  |

### `[mcp.packages.credential_probe]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `identity_patterns` | `['(^\|_)(USER\|USERNAME\|USER_NAME\|LOGIN\|EMAIL\|ACCOUNT)$']` | Names that carry *who* logs in.  Beside a stand-in credential they are replaced with placeholder_user, and for an anonymous call removed: a stand-in password beside the real user name is a failed login for a real account, and enough of those lock it.  build.opensuse.org's login, which worked on Oct 14, began answering every call with an error page the next day. |
| `placeholder_user` | `"initialize-claude-ai-stand-in-user"` |  |
| `max_refused_logins_per_credential` | `2` | Refused real logins per credential per run; once spent, that credential is not tried again in the run, so the run's own checks never add to the refusals that lock an account.  0 sets no limit. |
| `volatile_patterns` | `[ …` | Parts of a failure that differ between two launches of the same failure -- timestamps, process ids, addresses, temporary paths -- removed before the trial with a stand-in credential is compared with the one without.  If they then read the same, the credential is proved not to be the missing piece, and the server is not recorded as waiting for it. |
| `placeholder` | `"initialize-claude-ai-stand-in-not-a-real-credential"` |  |
| `timeout_seconds` | `"${cfg:mcp.packages.trial_timeout_seconds}"` |  |
| `companion_suffixes` | `["USER", "USERNAME", "LOGIN"]` | A credential in parts.  When the stand-in for the declared secret moves the failure on to another credential-shaped complaint, the server used it and wants the rest -- osc-mcp went from "password not found" to "user not set" once OSC_MCP_PASSWORD held a stand-in, because it reads OSC_MCP_USER too. The other part is looked for among variables the complaint names, then the secret's own prefix with each suffix below (OSC_MCP_PASSWORD -> OSC_MCP_USER), each tried with the stand-in, at most max_companion_trials launches.  The part that completes it is declared as a slot beside the secret.  0 trials turns this off. |
| `max_companion_trials` | `3` |  |

### `[mcp.bridge.generated]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `filename_template` | `"mcp_bridge_{slug}.py"` | The generated bridge is a self-contained Python stdio server. |
| `interpreter` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_BRIDGE_PYTHON:-}"` | Which interpreter the bridge is registered with. Empty resolves it at generation time to an absolute path -- this program's own interpreter -- and writes that into .mcp.json. Never the bare word "python3". The bridge is proved during discovery and launched later by Claude Code, in a different process with a different PATH, so a bare name is resolved a second time and can land on a different interpreter: a Homebrew, pyenv or conda Python ahead of the system one.  The bridge is standard-library only, so it still runs -- but it runs with that interpreter's certificate store, and against a target whose certificate is signed by an internal authority every call then fails TLS verification, which reads like the target being unreachable and is not. |
| `interpreter_names` | `["python3", "python"]` | Looked up only if the interpreter above is unset and this program's own interpreter cannot be determined. |
| `ca_bundle` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_BRIDGE_CA_BUNDLE:-}"` | PEM bundle the bridge verifies TLS against. Empty auto-detects from the list below; set it to pin one file. The bridge never disables verification -- an unverifiable peer is not a verified one -- so an internal CA is accepted by naming the bundle that contains it, not by turning the check off. |
| `max_tools` | `40` | The system trust stores, in the order they are tried; the first that exists wins. These are where a distribution puts the authorities the host has been told to trust, including any the administrator added -- a superset of what an interpreter ships with, so naming one never weakens verification. An empty |
| `safe_methods` | `["GET", "HEAD", "OPTIONS"]` | Only expose these HTTP methods as tools unless the operator opts in. |
| `accept` | `"*/*"` | The Accept header a generated bridge sends for an operation whose description names exactly one media type it does not (one that does is asked for exactly that type; several documented types get this value too).  Written into the manifest; MCP_BRIDGE_ACCEPT overrides it at launch.  ONE value, never a weighted list: Open Build Service answered a logged-in request carrying "application/json, application/xml;q=0.9, */*;q=0.8" -- or any other multi-value Accept -- with its HTML 404 page, while every single value (*/*, application/xml, even application/json) got the XML.  Anonymous calls got 401 either way, so a run without credentials never saw it.  Asking for JSON alone once got 406 from the same API: */* refuses nothing. |
| `accept_retry_statuses` | `[404, 406, 415]` | A generated bridge retries a read-only call answered with one of these statuses once with each value of accept_fallbacks it has not sent yet, and keeps the first value that works for the rest of its session -- an API whose gateway rejects a request's form says so with a 404/406/415 page, not with the API's own answer.  Calls that may change something are never repeated. |
| `accept_fallbacks` | `["*/*"]` |  |
| `include_mutating_methods` | `false` |  |

### `[mcp.registration.claude_check]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `command` | `["{claude}", "-p", "--output-format", "stream-json", "--verbose", "…` |  |
| `prompt` | `"Call the tool {tool} exactly once with these arguments: {arguments…` |  |
| `max_turns` | `4` |  |
| `retries_on_failure` | `1` | A failed check is asked again this many times before it is believed: Claude Code words a tool's error its own way (github-com's get_me, slow on a first connection, came back as "has an output schema but did not return structured content"), and one session's answer is not a verdict on the entry. |
| `timeout_seconds` | `180` |  |
| `model` | `""` |  |
| `connect` | `true` | Before any tool is asked, and whatever the credentials: Claude Code itself connects to the entry.  It is added to a throw-away configuration directory holding a copy of settings.json (so its env applies) and `claude mcp get` reports its status -- Claude Code's loader, environment and start-up wait, no model request.  gitlab-example-net's mcp-graphql started in the trial and timed out after Claude Code's 30 s; the only check through Claude Code was skipped because no tool could be called without a token.  An entry registered with its credential slot empty that answers with one of waiting_markers is waiting, not broken. |
| `connect_timeout_seconds` | `300` |  |
| `status_pattern` | `'(?im)^\s*status:\s*(?P<status>.+)$'` |  |
| `waiting_markers` | `["needs authentication", "401", "unauthorized"]` |  |
| `read_failure_reason` | `true` | How a service is logged in to -- every way it offers, and which to use build.example.net answers Basic; its API host api.example.net answers Signature (requests signed with the operator's SSH key, which osc does) -- and the program read only the first challenge of the first host.  Now every WWW-Authenticate challenge is read, on the target and on its API hosts (api_host_patterns: {domain} is the last two labels, {host} the target), at the product's protected_paths or at challenge_paths.  Each scheme is classified below; a client-only one is never "a token sent under that word".  The method used is the first feasible one in method_order; the rest are named as alternatives.  read_challenges = false asks nothing. Why a connection failed, read from `claude mcp list` (`claude mcp get` says only "Failed to connect") and classed by its words, so the repair fits it: openqa-example-net was "could not connect" while the listing said UNABLE_TO_GET_ISSUER_CERT_LOCALLY -- a trust failure, repaired by giving Claude Code the trust ([mcp.trust.consumer]) and asking again.  First match wins; anything else is "server". |
| `withdraw_not_mcp` | `true` | Claude Code reached a URL entry and what answered is not MCP (failure class not_mcp): the entry is taken out of .mcp.json again (the one it replaced comes back), its URL closes no tier, and the address is handed over. |
| `list_command` | `["{claude}", "mcp", "list"]` |  |

### `[mcp.verification]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `withhold_unsupplied` | `true` | A trial launched *without* a credential is launched without it: every credential it is not given -- the pending variables, the slots left out for want of a value, every declared credential slot, and each credential-named variable the launched source reads -- is removed from what it would inherit from this run's environment (a stand-in or real login it is given on purpose is kept).  github.com's "no credential" trial authenticated with a token the child inherited, and the run concluded the token was optional. |
| `learn_job_when_judging` | `true` | What the address is (its product and API kinds) is known before any candidate for it is judged: when nothing has recorded it yet, the verifier asks the learner the address's pipeline left (both modes, every path).  Agent mode's fallback package stage skipped it, and gitlab.example.net's mcp-graphql was verified on "describe the API" alone, then dropped by a re-check that knew the address was a GitLab. |
| `recheck_proved_tasks` | `true` | The final re-check asks what proved each server -- the usage tasks that passed -- and nothing new.  One that still answers but no longer does what proved it is said so, never "no longer answers"; one that now waits for a credential is kept, waiting.  A job that changed is judged again before the choice (rejudge_stale_verdicts). |
| `rejudge_stale_verdicts` | `true` | A verdict reached under a job that has since changed (the address identified after its candidates were judged) is reached again, under what the address is, before anything is chosen or written. |
| `heal_transport` | `true` | Calls that never reached the service -- a trust store it cannot read, a name it cannot resolve, a refused connection -- are not a server failing its job. With heal_transport, an existing entry whose calls fail this way has every trust-store variable its runtime reads that names a missing, empty or chain-less file pointed at a bundle that works, and is proved again before it is judged: smelt-example-net's working mcp-graphql met "fetch failed" on another machine and was replaced. |
| `heal_transport_everywhere` | `true` | ...for every stage's candidates too -- a package, a generated bridge, an agent's proposal: gitlab.example.net's mcp-graphql met "fetch failed" twice (Node ignores the host's trust store) and the address ended with nothing. |
| `resolve_from_claude_settings` | `true` | A trial resolves an entry's ${NAME} from Claude Code's own settings.json env too, as Claude Code does -- this program keeps the credentials an entry carried there (mcp.registration.keep_credentials_in). |
| `no_credential_call_timeout_seconds` | `20` | A tool call made with no credential at all (a trial before any is offered) waits at most this long for its answer: a server that waits for a token may never answer, and github-mcp-server held its address for four minutes that way.  No answer is "unproven", never an error.  0 keeps the normal wait. |
| `no_credential_give_up_after_silence` | `true` | ...and once one such call goes unanswered, the rest of that session gives up at once: a server waiting for a token answers none of them. |
| `use_supplied_values` | `true` | A variable a candidate reads that nothing sets, but that an existing entry for the address supplies (its ${NAME:-value}, or a literal under that key), is tried with that value: the operator gave it.  build-example-net's new SSH-key bridge read BUILD_EXAMPLE_NET_USERNAME, which only the old entry carried. |
| `align_slots_to_source` | `true` | Before a trial, a credential slot the launched script's own source never reads, beside exactly one credential variable it reads and nobody declared, is renamed to that one (sd.example.com's agent bridge read JIRA_PERSONAL_TOKEN; its slot had another name, and the token never arrived). |
| `transport_failure_markers` | `[ …` |  |
| `enabled` | `true` |  |
| `public_call_login_markers` | `['\b40[13]\b', "must be authenticated", 'unauthori[sz]ed', "authent…` | A bridge's "needs no login" call answered with a login refusal is the API asking for a login there too -- the bridge reaches it and waits for a credential; it is not broken.  sd.example.com's servicedeskapi/info came to answer 401. |
| `judge_existing_as_written` | `true` | An existing registration counts as answering only the way Claude Code runs it: not reported failing by `claude mcp list`, and starting when launched exactly as written.  The run's own trial drops a variable nothing sets where Claude Code passes the literal ${NAME}: bugzilla-opensuse-org's CLI copy crashed on '${BUGZILLA_AUTH_MODE}' and was kept as "answered during this run".  A broken one is replaced, in the file and the CLI -- never kept in place. |
| `require_initialize` | `true` | Require a successful JSON-RPC initialize handshake. |
| `require_tool_listing` | `true` | Also require tools/list (or resources/list) to return without error. |
| `allow_empty_tools` | `false` | Accept a server that advertises nothing at all -- no tools, no resources, no prompts.  Off: an MCP server Claude Code cannot call anything on is not a result worth registering. |
| `client_name_pattern` | `"^[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]{1,64}$"` | What the client accepts in the tools a server lists.  The client is the judge, so its rules are written here rather than in code.  An input property key that breaks client_name_pattern makes the Anthropic API refuse EVERY request of a Claude Code session once that tool is loaded -- openSUSE's osc-mcp declares "path_repository jsonschema:" on search_packages, and every message after it failed with "Property keys should match pattern".  Claude Code rewrites MCP tool names itself (mcp__<server>__<tool>), so the tool-name rule is empty by default; set it for a client that does not. |
| `client_tool_name_pattern` | `""` |  |
| `schema_problems` | `"refuse"` | What to do with a server whose tools break those rules: refuse  not registered, as a server that does not work -- the default, because registering it breaks the session it is registered into warn    registered, with the tool and key named in the report off     not checked |
| `require_round_trip` | `true` | Require a request sent AFTER the handshake to come back with its own id -- tools/list where there is one, otherwise the spec's own `ping`.  This is what distinguishes a working session from an endpoint that can only say hello. |
| `handshake_timeout_seconds` | `20` |  |
| `stdio_startup_timeout_seconds` | `25` |  |
| `stdio_session_timeout_seconds` | `240` | Ceiling on one whole stdio session -- initialize, the capability lists and the round trip together.  Each request is bounded by the timeout it was launched with (mcp.packages.trial_timeout_seconds for a trial); this bounds their sum, so a server answering every request just inside its limit cannot hold a trial for many times that.  Never shorter than the per-request timeout.  0 = no ceiling beyond the per-request one. |
| `stdio_shutdown_grace_seconds` | `2` | Seconds a stdio server is given to exit on its own once its stdin is closed, before its whole process group is taken down run.stop_signals (each followed by run.stop_grace_seconds).  The shutdown is bounded end to end: a server that ignored stdin closing, or a launcher's grandchild holding the output pipe, once held jira.example.com's package stage -- and the run -- open indefinitely. |
| `final_recheck` | `true` | Re-verify each server once more at the end of the phase. |
| `prefer_https` | `true` | An http:// endpoint that also answers over https:// is used over https://: a credential is never sent in the clear, and services refuse it -- openqa-example-net was written as http://openqa.example.net/mcp and answered "personal access token can only be used via HTTPS". |
| `https_when_it_answers` | `true` | It moves to https:// whenever the https side answers at all -- also with a page asking to come back later (a bot check) -- not only with a handshake or a login wall: whether it takes a login is often not known yet, and a credential must never be what finds that out over cleartext. |
| `launcher_retries` | `1` | A launcher's own momentary failure is no verdict on the entry: two "npx -y mcp-graphql@2.0.4" starting together on a fresh npm cache -- one read the package before the other finished installing it ("npm error enoent ... _npx/.../package.json") -- and gitlab-example-net's entry was called "does not start" and replaced.  Such a launch is retried after a pause. |
| `launcher_retry_pause_seconds` | `3.0` |  |
| `launcher_transient_patterns` | `[ …` |  |
| `launcher_warming_patterns` | `['(?i)\bdownloading\b', '(?i)\binstalled \d+ packages?\b', '(?i)\br…` | A launcher still fetching what the server needs (a cold uv or npm cache) is slow, not broken: a launch that failed while its output showed a download is launched once more with launcher_warm_timeout_seconds to finish, and judged by its answer.  confluence-example-com's mcp-atlassian "did not start" while uvx was downloading pydantic-core, and a server taking 87 s was written instead. |
| `launcher_warm_timeout_seconds` | `300.0` |  |

### `[mcp.verification.runtime_tuning]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | A variable that tunes the runtime rather than configures the server fits the machine it was written on, and .mcp.json travels to every other. smelt-example-net carried NODE_OPTIONS=--network-family-autoselection-attempt- timeout=30000 from an old entry: 5 s on the machine that ran the program, 53 s or more on the next -- past Claude Code's 30 s start-up wait.  Every stdio candidate carrying one is launched once without; when it does as well (starts, same tools, same credential wait) and starts no slower than start_slack_seconds later, the setting is dropped.  Matched whole. |
| `runtime_option_variables` | `[ …` |  |
| `start_slack_seconds` | `2.0` |  |
| `unknown_job_keeps` | `true` | "As well" is the job: the usage tasks and real calls must give the same result without the setting, not only the handshake -- smelt-example-net's mcp-graphql started without NODE_OPTIONS on a machine whose network needed it for every real call, and the working entry was replaced.  When nothing showed the job, the setting stays (for this machine only). |
| `per_machine` | `true` | A runtime setting that stays is this machine's, not the file's: the entry reads ${machine_variable_template:-} and the value goes into this machine's Claude Code settings env.  smelt-example-net's NODE_OPTIONS was needed on one machine and held the start past 30 s on the next -- a literal served neither. |
| `machine_variable_template` | `"ICA_MCP_{SLUG}_{KEY}"` |  |
| `flag_start_hazards` | `true` | The final file check flags a runtime setting holding a wait at or past margin x Claude Code's start-up wait ([mcp.registration.client_timeout]): a number after a flag naming a timeout, milliseconds from 1000 up. |
| `drop_samples` | `3` | A setting is dropped only when every one of drop_samples launches without it does the job as well -- smelt-example-net's NODE_OPTIONS went on one, and Claude Code's check 20 s later failed every call with "fetch failed".  When Claude Code's own use of an entry fails the way a network does (restore_on) after a drop, the setting comes back for this machine only (per-machine variable) and the check is asked again; it goes again if that did not help. |
| `restore` | `true` |  |
| `restore_on` | `['fetch failed', 'ETIMEDOUT', 'ECONNRESET', 'ECONNREFUSED', 'ENETUN…` |  |

File does not exist" -- a deleted /tmp bundle a login shell exported.  The last stderr line matching a class (first class that matches wins) is attached to each failed call and kept on the result; "trust" is repaired (mcp.repair.classes.trust_file), "transport" is a network fault -- neither is blamed on the server. |

### `[mcp.verification.server_credential]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | `true` | A stdio candidate with no way to send a login (no declared slot, no credential setting, none carried in a form) is given the variable its own server reads a login from -- found in its code (mcp.env_contract: a script or an installed package): gitlab.example.net's graphql-mcp-server reads API_ACCESS_TOKEN, mcp-bugzilla reads BUGZILLA_API_KEY.  Both were written with no credential at all because they answered anybody.  The slot is trialled like a declared one and written optional when the server works without it; an anonymous answer never costs the login.  One credential read is that variable; among several, the one naming the address's product; several still (a user name and a password, a choice of logins) is none, and is reported (report_ambiguous).  Applies to every path's candidate: agent, traditional, existing, repaired. |
| `report_ambiguous` | `true` |  |
| `from_sibling_entries` | `true` | When its own code says nothing (a binary, an image, a package not on disk): the one credential key the same package's other entries read -- the file's, and those written earlier in this run.  bugzilla-example-com's mcp-bugzilla read BUGZILLA_API_KEY; bugzilla-opensuse-org's was written with none. |

### `[mcp.verification.login_check]`

| Key | Default | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `mode` | `"${INITIALIZE_CLAUDE_AI_MCP_LOGIN_CHECK:-pending}"` |  |
| `tool_patterns` | `[ …` | Tried in this order; the first that matches a listed tool is called. |
| `never_patterns` | `[ …` | Names that may change something, whatever an annotation or pattern says. |
| `read_verbs` | `["get", "list", "search", "show", "describe", "read", "info", "find…` | Names beginning with one of these verbs are eligible too (after the patterns above and anything annotated read-only), unless never_patterns matches.  One accepted call proves only that call's code path: osc-mcp's API tools accepted OSC_MCP_API=https://api.opensuse.org, and only search_packages rejected it. |
| `arguments` | `{ "^(pattern\|query\|q\|search\|search_?term\|term\|keyword\|text)$" = "{p…` | Values for required arguments, by argument-name pattern.  {product} is the target's product word, {host} its host.  An argument no pattern fills takes the value the tool's own schema offers (default, const, first example or enum value); a tool with an argument neither can fill is not called, and is named in the report as not exercised. |
| `max_calls` | `3` | How many tools may be called.  Every one is judged: a refusal from any call outranks acceptance from another, acceptance needs a call that returned content, and a "misconfigured" answer from any is kept beside the verdict. |
| `empty_answers_prove_nothing` | `true` | A successful answer that is structurally empty -- an empty list or object, an object whose list fields (empty_list_fields) are all empty, a zero total (empty_total_fields), blank text -- proves nothing about access.  sd.example.com's customer account got [] from jira_get_all_projects while every issue lookup went to the portal; taken as "accepted", it settled the address on a server the account cannot use. |
| `empty_total_fields` | `["total", "size", "count", "totalCount", "total_count", "totalSize"]` |  |
| `empty_list_fields` | `["values", "items", "results", "issues", "projects", "data", "nodes…` |  |
| `no_identity_patterns` | `[ …` | A successful answer that says *who* is calling is nobody proves no login: gitlab.example.net answered {"currentUser": null} -- its server sent no token -- and was counted as working.  Regexes over the answer's text, by behaviour, never a product: a null identity field, an "authenticated: false". |
| `unproved_settles` | `false` | Does a server whose access stays unproved (every answer empty or unchecked) end the tier search when the target also serves a bridgeable API kind the server does not speak?  false keeps searching, so that API is bridged and checked; a candidate with proven access then takes the slot.  With no such alternative detected, nothing changes. |
| `check_in_use` | `true` | Also check the credential an *existing* entry uses right now -- a literal it holds, or the default of its ${NAME:-...} while NAME is unset.  It is what Claude Code sends every time it loads the file: sd.example.com's entry held one its service refused, and with the exported variable unset the run said nothing about it.  The value is kept in memory for this one read-only call, redacted from every log, and never written -- the entry still reads ${NAME}. |
| `borrow_in_use` | `true` | Offer that value to the other candidates for the *same host* whose only missing credential is a single one -- a bridge generated for sd.example.com's customer API asks for SD_EXAMPLE_COM_TOKEN, and the token the existing entry already uses for sd.example.com is the one to try.  Same host only, the one read-only call only, never written. |
| `borrow_held` | `true` | What the operator already exports for the address (mcp.discovery.auth.inventory) fills a waiting server's slots for its login check -- each slot by what it holds, all or none -- and, accepted, the entry reads those variables (a slot taking "Authorization:Basic <base64 of user:password>" gets that form with a ${...} reference).  With nothing held for it, a login held for another address of the same organisation is tried once (single sign-on), only suggested. A refusal from a credential other hosts' entries send (a token issued by another instance) is not a verdict on this address: "foreign_credential". |
| `no_access_settles` | `false` | Does a server whose account has *no API access* end the tier descent, the way a credential wall does?  It should not: the credential is valid, the account is simply not allowed to use the API that server speaks -- and another server, for an API the account can use, may be one tier down.  sd.example.com's customer account could not use the core Jira API but could use the Service Desk customer API.  A rejected credential still settles (a new token is the fix). |
| `unconfirmed_rejection_settles` | `false` | Does a refusal from a candidate that chose for itself how to send the credential -- a bridge an agent wrote, with no API description, 401 challenge, configured `security` or published code behind its method -- end the descent?  It should not: the 401 is evidence about the bridge as much as about the credential.  sd.example.com's agent-written bridge was refused and the report blamed the token, while the run's own bridge, sending it the documented way, was never built.  And when the same credential is accepted by one candidate and refused by another, the refusing one is discarded as broken whatever this says. |
| `compare_with_standin` | `true` | When every call fails alike with the credential (the same HTTP status), the same launch is run once more with a stand-in in every credential slot.  If the stand-in is refused (401) or answered differently, the login was recognised and the service has no account behind it: no API access, with its own remedy (remedies.no_account).  Not before the request's form is ruled out: build.opensuse.org answered its entry's login with an HTML 404 for every path while no login and a made-up one got 401 -- and the account existed; the bridge's multi-value Accept header was the cause ([mcp.verification.request_forms] runs first when the failure is a gateway's web page).  The stand-in's answers are compared, never kept. |
| `compare_with_anonymous` | `true` | Ask the same calls with no credential at all, after a login check that was accepted or refused.  An accepted call anybody can make proves nothing about the login (build-example-net "worked" for days on get_about, which build.example.net answers anyone); a refusal identical to an anonymous caller's may mean the credential was never sent (remedies.same_as_anonymous).  Nobody is logged in for this comparison, so no account is put at risk. |
| `temporary_markers` | `[ …` | "Try again later" is never a verdict: an answer with one of these markers or status codes -- a rate limit, a gateway or service down for now, a timeout -- is asked once more after temporary_retry_seconds (at most temporary_retry_max_seconds), and if it is still temporary the result is inconclusive: it never counts as a failed call, never fails a usage task, never makes an existing entry unusable and never starts a repair. bugzilla.example.com's working entry got "429 Too Many Requests" and was replaced. A connection that dropped or stalled on the way is the same -- the service was never asked: github.com's get_me met "TLS handshake timeout" and "unexpected EOF" on a slow first connection, and the run took the token for refused. "fetch failed" and certificate errors are not here: they are a trust store to repair (transport_failure_markers, heal_transport), not a moment to wait out. |
| `temporary_statuses` | `[429, 502, 503, 504]` |  |
| `temporary_retry_seconds` | `5` |  |
| `temporary_retry_max_seconds` | `30` |  |
| `try_without_credential` | `true` | A server whose read calls succeed with no credential at all works without a login -- a public service (bugzilla.opensuse.org) -- and is counted as working: its credential becomes optional, written ${NAME:-}, never waited for.  try_without_credential asks those calls when the credential is missing; public_works_without_login applies the same when the anonymous comparison above finds the answers identical.  Nobody is logged in for either. |
| `public_works_without_login` | `true` |  |
| `public_needs_the_job` | `true` | ...but only when what answered is the server's job: a usage task passed with no credential.  A call anybody may make (build.example.net's /about) with no task applying proves nothing, and the credential stays required -- mcp-openapi-proxy was written with EXTRA_HEADERS "${…:-}" that way, refused on every real call. |
| `job_done_is_no_login_needed` | `true` | A declared credential slot is not proof a login is needed.  A server whose usage tasks passed with nothing in its slot did the job anonymously: the slot is optional (${NAME:-}), whatever its login tool answered -- smelt.example.net's mcp-graphql was proposed with HEADERS and waited for it, while every task it fits passed without.  A refusal still keeps it waiting. |
| `probe_settings` | `true` | A read tool nobody could call (a required argument nobody could fill) is asked once with stand-in arguments, only to learn whether it accepts its settings: a setting is checked before the arguments are used.  osc-mcp's search_packages alone read OSC_MCP_API and was never called, so the address form it rejected shipped.  The answer is read for misconfiguration_markers and nothing else -- never a login verdict.  setting_probe_values: a stand-in per JSON type. |
| `setting_probe_max` | `12` |  |
| `setting_probe_values` | `{ string = "initialize-claude-ai-probe", integer = 1, number = 1, b…` |  |
| `flag_unread_credentials` | `true` | A credential variable that what the entry launches never reads -- its source never mentions the name, and reads a credential under another one -- is a credential that is never sent.  build.example.net's login sat in BUILD_EXAMPLE_NET_BASE64_OF_USER_PASSWORD; mcp-openapi-proxy reads API_KEY and EXTRA_HEADERS. | `identity_tool_patterns` | `['(^\|_)(get_)?(me\|myself\|whoami\|current_user)$', '(^\|_)(get_)?my_(a…` | A tool reading the logged-in account's own record that answers 404 *in the API's own form* means the same: no account for this login. A refusal, an empty answer or one accepted call keeps the other verdicts. |
| `failed_calls_min` | `2` |  |
| `reuse_variable_names` | `true` | When a candidate is proved with the credential *another* entry for the same host already reads, its entry reads that entry's variable too -- one instance's token, one export -- instead of a new name for the same value. |

A successful listing is never read for markers -- an issue numbered 4031 is not a 403. |

| `misconfiguration_markers` | `[ …` | Wordings of a failed answer that mean a *setting* is written in a form the server rejects -- an address with a scheme where it wants a bare host. | `status_outranks_wording` | `true` | Markers are matched case-insensitively, as whole words where they begin and end with a letter or digit. One status only; status_pattern finds it, status_verdicts says what it means. |
| `status_verdicts` | `{ "401" = "rejected", "403" = "no_access" }` |  |

| `confirm_by_own_record` | `true` | A refused single-secret login is asked once more of the service itself: a protected_paths page of the address's product, sent as its catalogue login says (sent_as).  401 there is the credential refused, 403 an account without access -- whatever the tool called it. |
| `rejected_markers` | `[ …` | Wordings of an answer that mean the credential itself was refused. |
| `no_access_markers` | `[ …` | Wordings of an answer that mean the service took the request and sent this account somewhere other than its API -- a portal, a login page -- or forbade it. |
| `content_outranks_scoped_refusal` | `true` | A NO_ACCESS answer carrying one of these is about the *account* -- sent to a customer portal, a login or a sign-on page -- and outranks a call that was accepted with content. | `account_wide_markers` | `["/servicedesk/customer", "/login", "/sso/"]` |  |
| `name_other_service_login` | `true` | A login one address refused that a service of *another* organisation accepted is named as that service's login (compared by fingerprints of its secret parts, never by value): build.example.net was given the build.opensuse.org login. | `name_other_routes` | `true` | A login refused on one route is answered with the other routes the service offered, each with its own setup step: build.example.net refused a Example login over basic auth while api.example.net asked for an SSH-key signature, a route never named. |

| `borrow_same_part` | `true` | A credential an existing entry uses is offered to a new server only for a slot holding the same kind of value (mcp.discovery.auth.inventory parts): the password build.example.net's old entry carried was offered as the new bridge's USERNAME, and the key route was wrongly recorded as refused. |
| `same_as_anonymous_is_not_a_refusal` | `true` | A refusal identical to what an anonymous caller gets shows nothing reached the server -- the credential may never have arrived (a slot the server does not read).  It is not counted against the credential's allowance of refused logins, not recorded as refused in the login history, and ranks like a credential still missing, so the next candidate is still offered it. |
| `job_refused_markers` | `["query too large", "query is too large", "query has complexity", "…` | Failures that say the service refused the query a tool sent -- too large, too complex, too deep -- rather than the caller: no credential can make that tool work, so the server is a failure, never "waiting for a credential". gitlab.example.net answered mcp-graphql's currentUser with "Query too large", with a valid token and without one. |
| `missing_credential_markers` | `[ …` | Wordings of a refusal that mean no credential reached the server at all -- the variable was unset, no key file existed -- rather than that one was refused.  When every login an address was asked with failed this way, the report says nothing on this machine can log in to it and names, per server, what to supply -- never "check that your login works": no login was tried. |
